summary: The @mention grammar (HANDLE_BODY interior charset and the MENTION_RE leading guard) has no absolute pin anywhere in the suite. The only generator-driven test is the parseMentions <-> isMentionableHandle equivalence, which is a tautology under co-drift: both sides are derived from the same HANDLE_BODY constant, so any widening or narrowing of the grammar moves producer and predicate together and the parity holds. The mention grammar is what live_push.mention_filter uses to decide which inbound messages reach the agent, so it is a delivery/security boundary with effectively zero coverage of its accepted character set.
failure: Mutation 1 (narrowing), applied to mentions.ts:5 `[A-Za-z0-9._-]*` -> `[A-Za-z0-9.-]*`: 41 test files / 2109 tests all pass. Under it, `identity.handle: 'ctx_payments'` with `live_push: {enabled: true, mention_filter: true}` now FAILS config load with 'no message can ever produce that handle', and `parseMentions('hi @ctx_payments')` returns `['ctx']` instead of `['ctx_payments']` — every message addressed to an underscore handle is silently dropped by the mention filter. Mutation 2 (widening), applied simultaneously: `[A-Za-z0-9._-]*` -> `[A-Za-z0-9.:_-]*` AND the guard `(?:^|[^A-Za-z0-9_.@-])` -> `(?:^|[^A-Za-z0-9@])`: again 2109/2109 pass. Under it `parseMentions('see config.@alice')` returns `['alice']` (previously `[]`) and `parseMentions('build-@bob')` returns `['bob']`, so mention_filter now surfaces messages nobody addressed. mentions.test.ts only pins '.' and '-' as interior chars (line 37) and '_' only in the TRAILING position (line 32), where both the original and the mutant answer 'bob'.
remediation: Add an absolute grammar table to mentions.test.ts that does not read HANDLE_BODY: one row per character class, each asserting the exact parsed output — interior '_' , '.', '-' accepted ('a_b', 'a.b', 'a-b'); ':' , '/', '+', '@', whitespace NOT accepted (parse of '@a:b' is ['a']); and a guard table pinning that '.', '-', '_', '@' immediately before '@' suppress the mention while '(', ' ', '*', ',', newline, start-of-string do not. Keep the existing parity test — it guards the mismatch class — but it must not be the only grammar test.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a grammar whose only test is agreement between two derivations of the same constant'. Parameterize over a table of (character, position in {leading, interior, trailing, guard-before-@}) -> expected verdict, with the expected verdict written as a literal, never derived from HANDLE_BODY/MENTION_RE. Widen the config.test.ts HANDLES list and the mentions.test.ts CANDIDATES list into one shared corpus, and add a mutation guard: for each of a handful of one-character edits to the interior class and to the guard class, at least one test must fail. The same recipe applies to any other place in this package where a producer and its predicate are compiled from one shared source string.

summary: MAX_GLOB_LEN's VALUE is unpinned. Every test that touches it derives its probe from the constant (stated-bounds.test.ts:51-57 builds an `'a'.repeat(len-1)` handle from `b.bound`; identity-filter.test.ts:139 uses `MAX_GLOB_LEN + 50`; transport/tools.ts:316 uses `.max(MAX_GLOB_LEN)`), so the constant can move by a factor of 32 in either direction and the whole suite stays green. It is a documented user-facing capacity (the `parley_list_users` filter length limit) and simultaneously the DoS bound on the O(P*S) glob walk, so both directions matter.
failure: Mutation `export const MAX_GLOB_LEN = 256;` -> `= 8` in identity-filter.ts:11: 2105/2105 tests pass. Under it, `parley_list_users({ filter: 'claude-agent-*' })` (14 chars) is rejected by the tool input schema (`z.string().max(8)` -> validation error), and any code path calling matchGlob directly gets a silent `false` for a filter that plainly matches — verified: `matchGlob('claude-agent-*','claude-agent-payments')` is true at 256 and the schema rejects the same filter at 8. The reverse mutation (raising it) removes the stated bound on match work with equal silence.
remediation: Pin the value where it is a promise, not only where it is a bound: assert `MAX_GLOB_LEN >= 128` (or the exact documented number) alongside a literal round-trip — e.g. a realistic 32-char filter like 'claude-agent-oncall-payments-*' must be accepted by the tool schema and must match, written as literals rather than repeat(MAX_GLOB_LEN - k).
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'documented capacity constant whose every probe is derived from itself'. Add one parameterized table over the package's exported capacity constants — MAX_GLOB_LEN, MAX_MATCH_INPUT, MAX_POST_TOPICS, MIN_HASH_LEN, MAX_AMBIGUITY — with a literal expected value and a literal realistic input that must be accepted, so shrinking or inflating any of them reddens. (MAX_MATCH_INPUT at 8 already fails 49 tests and MIN_HASH_LEN at 6 fails 8, so the table would only be adding the rows that are currently missing; the shape is what should be ratcheted so the next constant added gets a row for free.)

summary: seam.ts's fetchRecent JSDoc — the normative document a plugin author reads, and one that ships verbatim in the published `.d.ts` — states that 'the SQLite reference backend returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`' for a never-posted topic. The SQLite backend has not returned that for some time: its cursors are `<storeId>.<rowid>`, so a never-posted topic yields `<storeId>.0`.
failure: packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:231 returns `nextCursor: last?.cursor ?? mintCursor(storeId, resumeAfter ?? 0n)` and mintCursor (line 500) is `asCursor(`${storeId}.${rowid}`)`. So `fetchRecent({ topic: asTopic('never-posted') })` returns e.g. `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '9f3c1a2b.0' }`, not `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`. A plugin author calibrating 'what a replayable cold cursor looks like' against this doc is told a cursor is a bare integer string, which is exactly the assumption the seam's opacity rule (DESIGN §6) exists to forbid.
remediation: Either drop the concrete example (the contract — empty page plus a replayable nextCursor — is complete without it) or state it correctly and opaquely: 'the SQLite reference backend returns an empty page with a cold cursor naming position zero in its store'. Prefer dropping it: naming one backend's literal cursor in the seam doc invites exactly the value-shape assumption the seam forbids.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a seam/JSDoc claim about a specific backend's literal value'. Add a doc-conformance case in packages/conformance that, for every backend, asserts the never-posted-topic contract as a PROPERTY (empty messages; feeding nextCursor back as `since` yields [] and an equal cursor) and separately a source-lint that fails when seam.ts quotes a concrete cursor/id literal attributed to a named backend — the same lint shape source-hygiene.test.ts already uses for tracker ids and temporal comments.

summary: `catchup.block_max_ms` is `z.number().int().nonnegative()` with no upper bound, while its own JSDoc asserts the safety property it exists to provide: 'kept safely below MCP / client tool timeouts so a blocked call never trips them'. Every other cross-field safety property in this schema is enforced (presence.ttl_ms >= heartbeat_ms, mention_filter requires enabled, skip_permissions rejected); this one is prose only, so the schema accepts a value that falsifies its own docstring.
failure: `parseConfig({ identity: {handle:'h'}, topics:['t'], catchup: { block_max_ms: 3_600_000 } })` loads cleanly. transport/tools.ts:221 then computes `blockMs = Math.min(block_ms, deps.blockMaxMs)`, so `parley_fetch_recent({ topic, block_ms: 3600000 })` holds the tool call for one hour on an idle topic — past every MCP client tool timeout, producing exactly the 'blocked call trips the client timeout' outcome the field is documented to prevent, with no load-time warning.
remediation: Put a `.max()` on `block_max_ms` at a value that is actually below the client tool timeout the doc appeals to (e.g. 300_000), with an error message naming why. Fail fast at load rather than at the first long-poll.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a numeric knob whose docstring states a safety relationship the schema does not enforce'. Extend the existing 'config rejects a degenerate number in any numeric field' walker in config.test.ts with a third dimension: for every numeric leaf, a value one step past its documented ceiling must be refused, with the ceiling supplied by a per-field table so a knob added later without a ceiling shows up as a missing table row rather than as silent acceptance. Add block_max_ms to stated-bounds.test.ts's BOUNDS table once the cap exists.

summary: The barrel exports `safeName` and `MIN_HASH_LEN` but not `MAX_HASH_LEN`, while safeName's published JSDoc says 'Throws when `hashLen` is outside {@link MIN_HASH_LEN}…{@link MAX_HASH_LEN}'. The package `exports` map exposes only `.`, so an out-of-tree backend plugin — the audience the seam is a product for — can reference the floor symbolically but must hardcode the ceiling. index.test.ts's `kept` list pins MIN_HASH_LEN and is silent on MAX_HASH_LEN, cementing the asymmetry as 'intended surface'.
failure: `import { MAX_HASH_LEN } from '@sharptrick/parley-core'` is a TS2305/undefined at runtime, even though dist/topic-name.d.ts declares it and safeName's own doc comment (which ships in dist/index.d.ts's re-exported type) links to it. A third-party plugin validating an operator-supplied hashLen before calling safeName has to write the literal 40.

(Alternatively, if the ceiling is deliberately private, remove the {@link MAX_HASH_LEN} from the shipped doc and state the ceiling in prose — but exporting is the smaller change and matches the floor.)

Add a mechanical case to index.test.ts that scans every exported module's doc comments for `{@link X}` where X is a value (not a type-only or local) declaration and asserts `X in api` — so the next helper whose docs name an unexported constant is caught, rather than pinning MAX_HASH_LEN by name.

summary: `close()` called while a `listen()` is still in flight is a silent no-op, and the listen then completes anyway — leaving a bound socket and a presence loop that NO later close() can ever reach.
failure: Reproduced in /tmp/careening/worktrees/core-engine/packages/bridge-core/src/transport (throwaway probe, since deleted): `const app = createRemoteHttpApp(p, cfg, {insecureNoAuth:true}); const starting = app.listen(0); await app.close(); const s = await starting;` → logs `AFTER close(): listening = true port = 42159`; a SECOND `await app.close()` still logs `listening = true`; presence beat count grows from 6 to 12 across 240 ms of a 20 ms heartbeat. Trace: `listen` sets `httpServer = s` synchronously, but `s.listening` stays false until the `listening` event; `close()` reads `const s = httpServer; httpServer = undefined; starting = false; if (s === undefined || !s.listening) return;` and bails, then the listening event fires and the callback calls `announce()` on an app the operator already shut down. This is exactly the failure the neighbouring test's own docstring claims to prevent (http.test.ts:484 — "orphaning the first socket and its presence loop where no close() can ever reach them").
remediation: Add a `closed` latch set by `close()`. The `listen` success callback must check it: if closing was requested, close `s` (and do NOT `announce()`) before resolving/rejecting. Alternatively have `close()` await the in-flight listen promise and then run the normal close path. Same latch must gate `announce()`.
testUpgrade: The existing `remote HTTP: close() resolves in whatever order the lifecycle runs` table (http.test.ts:169) awaits every `listen-ok` before the next op, so it structurally cannot enter this window. Widen the op vocabulary to include a non-awaited start — e.g. `['listen-pending','close','await-listen']` — and parameterize the SAME table over BOTH composition roots (http `listen`/`close` and stdio `attach`/`shutdown`), asserting after every sequence: nothing bound, no presence beat count growth over several cadences, and the plugin disconnected. That guards the CLASS 'teardown interleaved with a start that has not settled', not just this ordering.

summary: `shutdown()` racing an in-flight `attach()` sets `toreDown` and finishes, but `attach` carries on and starts a presence loop AFTER teardown — and then RESOLVES, handing the caller a "successfully attached" bridge whose plugin is disconnected and whose server is closed, with a heartbeat loop no shutdown can stop.
failure: Reproduced with the same probe: `const bridge = await buildBridge(p, cfg); const attaching = bridge.attach(t); await bridge.shutdown(); await attaching;` → `attach` RESOLVES (no rejection logged), and the presence beat count grows 6 → 12 over 240 ms at a 20 ms heartbeat, i.e. the loop is still beating long after shutdown. Trace: `teardown()` latches `toreDown = true` and returns; `attach` never re-reads that latch after its `await server.connect(transport)` / `await startPushLoop(...)`, so `presence = startPresenceLoop(...)` (line 136) runs post-teardown and `shutdown()` is already a no-op. `parley_list_users` therefore reports a shut-down bridge as online for the whole TTL window, forever refreshed.
remediation: Re-check `toreDown` after every await inside `attach` (after `server.connect`, after `startPushLoop`, and immediately before assigning `presence`); if teardown already ran, roll back what this attach started and reject. Equivalently, have `teardown()` await the in-flight attach promise before running its steps.
testUpgrade: Same widened lifecycle-order table as the http finding, driven through the `roots` record already present at http.test.ts:433 so both composition roots share the rows. Add a row `['shutdown while attach is in flight', ['attach-pending','shutdown','await-attach']]` and assert (a) no presence beats after teardown, (b) attach either rejects or leaves a bridge whose second shutdown is still effective. Generalize the existing `%s rejects a second start that OVERLAPS the first` case (http.test.ts:511) from start-vs-start to start-vs-stop.

summary: `filterReachable` compiles and runs untrusted peer regexes per ROSTER ENTRY, and the number of roster entries is unbounded (only the 500-message page bounds it) — so the per-beat caps that make each source cheap are multiplied by ~500, and one writer wedges the single-threaded process for seconds per `parley_list_users` call.
failure: Measured in a throwaway vitest probe (since deleted): 500 presence beats, each with a DIFFERENT self-reported `handle` (the handle is untrusted and record-supplied, so one credential mints all 500) and 64 `postTopics` of `'(?:a|aa)'.repeat(16)+'q'.repeat(k)` — every one passes `isRedosSafeSource` — produce a 500-entry roster; `filterReachable(roster, {canPostTo:()=>false, mySubscribedTopics:['a'.repeat(64)]})` blocks for **3024 ms** of synchronous CPU. That scales linearly with the caller's subscribed-topic count (10 topics → ~30 s) and repeats on every call, with no cache. During it the event loop is dead: long-polls, presence beats and every other MCP request stall. `regex-safety.ts:18` states the ambiguity bound is PER SOURCE and the caller 'must also bound HOW MANY it holds', and `MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES`' JSDoc (presence.ts:54) claims it 'stops the per-beat caps from being multiplied by the presence page size … in the untrusted patterns filterReachable compiles' — that claim is false, because it caps instances per handle and nothing caps handles. The same unbounded entry count also lets `parley_list_users` return ~500 × 64 × 512 bytes of attacker strings into the agent's context when `limit` is omitted.
remediation: Bound the roster globally, not just per record: cap the number of roster entries `computeRoster` emits (freshest-first), and give `filterReachable` a single whole-call budget on compiled/evaluated peer patterns (compile once per call with an LRU keyed on the source string, and stop after N total tests). Also apply a default `limit` to `parley_list_users` output rather than only an optional one.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'untrusted presence history cannot exceed a CPU budget' case that generates the worst source the screen accepts (derive it from `packages/bridge-core/src/testing/regex-corpus.ts` rather than hard-coding) and sweeps the multiplying dimensions independently — distinct handles × instances per handle × postTopics per beat × caller topics — asserting `filterReachable`/`parley_list_users` wall time stays under a fixed budget and the serialized result stays under a byte cap. That guards the CLASS 'a per-record cap multiplied by an attacker-chosen record count', which is what the existing per-cap unit tests (MAX_RECORD_TOPICS, MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES, MAX_TOPIC_LEN) each pin one factor of and none pin the product of.

summary: `SeenSet` (public API, re-exported from index.ts:48) accepts `0` for either cap and then silently stops deduping instead of failing fast — the opposite of how the sibling bounds in this package behave.
failure: Reproduced: `new SeenSet(4096, 0)` → `firstSeen(t,'m1')` returns `true`, and `firstSeen(t,'m1')` again returns `true`, with `has(t,'m1') === false` — the bucket is evicted by the LRU loop before `record` writes into it, so the returned set/queue are detached. `new SeenSet(0, 256)` behaves the same via the per-topic queue shift. An embedder wiring `new SeenSet(cfg.a, cfg.b)` from a mis-set config gets every message re-emitted as a `<channel>` event forever, with no error and no log. `fetchRecentBlocking` (blocking-fetch.ts) throws `RangeError` on a non-positive `pollIntervalMs` and `startPresenceLoop` throws on a non-positive `heartbeatMs` for exactly this reason; `SeenSet` is the outlier.
remediation: Throw `RangeError` from the constructor when `maxPerTopic` or `maxTopics` is not a positive integer, matching `fetchRecentBlocking`/`startPresenceLoop`.
testUpgrade: One parameterized table over every core knob that must be positive — `SeenSet(maxPerTopic)`, `SeenSet(maxTopics)`, `BlockingFetchOptions.pollIntervalMs`, `BlockingFetchOptions.blockMs` (finite), `PresenceLoopOptions.heartbeatMs` — crossed with the degenerate values `[0, -1, NaN, Infinity, 0.5]`, asserting each REJECTS rather than degrading. That guards the CLASS 'a bound whose degenerate value silently turns the feature off', which currently has three guarded sites and one unguarded one.

summary: `hasLiveCredential` decides which DCR registration may be evicted at the MAX_CLIENTS cap by scanning only `access` and `refresh`. It ignores `pending` (an owner consent awaiting a passphrase) and `codes`/`redeeming` (an owner-approved authorization code not yet exchanged) — precisely the window in which the owner's client holds no token yet. The comment two lines below claims the opposite invariant: "Only ever evict a client with no live token, so that unauthenticated DCR spam cannot push the owner's consented client out of the map and lock them out."
failure: Reproduced in my worktree with a throwaway vitest file. (a) register('legit-claude'); await provider.authorize(owner, params, res)  [pending consent exists, no tokens]; then 150 unauthenticated register() calls -> clientsStore.getClient('legit-claude') === undefined. (b) same but after completeConsent() minted the code -> getClient('legit-claude') === undefined. Downstream: the SDK's token router runs `authenticateClient({clientsStore})` before any provider method, so the owner's browser follows the 302 back to Claude with a valid `code`, /token answers `invalid_client` 401, and the owner's consent and code are spent. Repeatable -> the only path that authorizes the bridge is denied. The attacker needs ~100 anonymous DCR posts inside the 5-minute consent window; /register is rate-limited at 20/hour per IP, so ~5 source addresses suffice, and a sustained flood keeps the table saturated so no timing is required.
remediation: Make the eviction predicate cover every state that names a client, not just the token maps: extend `hasLiveCredential` (rename it, e.g. `hasClientState`) to also return true when any unexpired `pending` consent, `codes` entry or `redeeming` entry carries that clientId. Keep the TemporarilyUnavailableError fallback for the all-in-use case.
testUpgrade: The existing guard is `oauth-provider.test.ts` "the DCR cap never evicts a client that is in use", whose ACTIVE_SHAPES table enumerates only token-holding shapes (access only / refresh only / both) — it is too narrow by construction. Widen that same table into a `CLIENT_STATES` table over EVERY store the provider keys by client_id, one row per store, each row a setup function that leaves the client in that state and nothing else: ['pending consent', p => p.authorize(owner,...)], ['unredeemed code', p => authorize+completeConsent], ['code mid-redemption', p => ...+challengeForAuthorizationCode], plus the three existing token rows. Assert per row that 150 spam registrations leave getClient(owner) defined AND that the spam clients are still shed. Add a structural row-count assertion (e.g. the table must have one row per private Map the provider declares) so a future store added to the provider fails the suite until it is represented.

summary: `fetchOidcDiscovery` passes `redirect: 'manual'` with a comment insisting it be kept ("so that a 3xx cannot move the trust root to another origin before the issuer check ever sees the document"). Nothing tests it: flipping it to `redirect: 'follow'` leaves all 802 auth tests green. The control is counted as coverage by the suite and by the comment, and is in fact unguarded.
failure: Mutation: `redirect: 'manual'` -> `redirect: 'follow'` in packages/bridge-core/src/auth/oidc-discovery.ts. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/auth` -> Tests 802 passed (802). A future refactor that drops the option, or a switch to a fetch wrapper that defaults to follow, ships silently: a loopback/dev issuer (the one deployment where discovery runs over plaintext http, explicitly permitted by assertTrustRootUrl) can then be 302'd to another origin whose document the issuer check never distinguishes from a direct answer.
remediation: No production-code change required. Add coverage that pins the option's effect, and consider asserting `res.redirected === false` after the fetch so the behaviour is enforced in code rather than only by a flag.
testUpgrade: Guard the class, not the flag: parameterize `oidc-discovery.test.ts` over a REDIRECTING_ISSUER table — one row per 3xx status (301/302/303/307/308) — where a stub fetch serves a Location pointing at a second in-process origin that hosts a perfectly-valid discovery document whose `issuer` equals the CONFIGURED issuer. Every row must assert `fetchOidcDiscovery` rejects. Widen the same generator to the other place the auth layer dereferences a trust root: assert `createOidcRemoteApp` refuses when the jwks_uri is served behind a redirect. Any test that only asserts the literal string 'manual' appears in the source is not a substitute.

summary: `terminalErrorHandler`'s `if (res.headersSent) { next(err); return; }` branch has no coverage. The module JSDoc opens with "Keep BOTH halves of this", but deleting the headersSent guard entirely keeps all 802 auth tests green — so only the half that renders a generic body is actually pinned.
failure: Mutation: delete the three-line `if (res.headersSent) { next(err); return; }` block from packages/bridge-core/src/auth/error-surface.ts. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core/src/auth` -> Tests 802 passed (802). Without the guard, an error raised after the response has begun (a StreamableHTTP transport failing mid-write on /mcp, or a failure after `res.redirect(302, ...)` on /parley/consent) makes `res.status(...).send(...)` throw ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT inside the error handler instead of delegating to Express's default handler, which is the only thing that destroys the socket — the client is left holding a truncated response on an unclosed connection.
remediation: No production-code change required; the branch is correct. Cover it so it cannot be deleted silently.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized ERROR_TIMING table to `error-surface.test.ts` with a route registered on a test app for each phase an error can arrive in — ['before any write', h => h(new Error('x'))], ['after res.write(partial)', ...], ['after res.end()', ...] — and assert per row: a body that never contains 'at ' / a filesystem path, and for the headersSent rows that the connection is destroyed rather than the handler throwing. Apply the same table to both front doors (createOAuthRemoteApp and createOidcRemoteApp) so a mode that forgets hardenErrorSurface is caught by the same rows.

summary: The Testing section states "`packages/bridge-core/src/auth/keycloak.e2e.test.ts` self-skips unless a realm answers at http://127.0.0.1:8080/realms/parley (override with PARLEY_KEYCLOAK_URL)". The file does the opposite by design: it self-skips ONLY on the explicit `PARLEY_E2E=0` opt-out, and when the realm is unreachable it registers a describe that THROWS ("This suite must not skip itself into a green run"). The doc never mentions PARLEY_E2E, and it contradicts docs/1.0-readiness.md, which advertises the no-self-skip gate as a 1.0 achievement.
failure: Read docs/keycloak-integration.md:210-216, then packages/bridge-core/src/auth/keycloak.e2e.test.ts:21 (`OPTED_OUT = process.env.PARLEY_E2E === '0'`) and :121-134 (the `else if (!(await waitForKeycloak()))` branch that throws). A contributor following the doc runs `npm test` on a machine with no Keycloak, waits READY_TIMEOUT_MS = 30s, and gets a red suite the doc told them would be skipped — with no doc mention of the PARLEY_E2E=0 escape it offers.

Extend `packages/bridge-core/src/auth/hygiene.test.ts` (which already owns the 'no suite may skip itself into green' scan) with a parameterized doc-consistency case: for every *.e2e.test.ts under packages/, if the file contains `describe.skip`, assert that every markdown file in docs/ and examples/ that names that file by path does NOT contain /self-skip|skips itself|automatically skip/ near the reference, and DOES name the env var the file actually reads. summary: `poll_interval_ms` is validated to death (11 rejection rows, a floor, a ceiling, a README table) but its EFFECT on the poll loop is never observed by any test. Replacing `let delay = this.pollIntervalMs;` with `let delay = 0;` — turning the live loop into a `setTimeout(tick, 0)` hot spin that re-queries the store ~1000x/s per topic per bridge process — leaves all 351 tests in the package green, including the whole conformance suite, the multi-process poll tests and the 'full poll batch reschedules immediately' table. The one constant whose JSDoc says 'below this the loop is a hot spin, not a poll' (MIN_POLL_INTERVAL_MS) therefore guards a value nothing downstream is graded on.
failure: Mutation: `packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:277` `let delay = this.pollIntervalMs;` -> `let delay = 0;`. Run `npx vitest run packages/bridge-sqlite --exclude '**/typecheck-coverage.test.ts'` -> `Test Files 15 passed (15) / Tests 351 passed (351)`. With `backend_config.poll_interval_ms: 60000` an operator gets a loop hammering the shared `.db` file every ~1 ms, contending for the WAL read lock with every peer bridge's `post()`, and no test anywhere goes red. The nearest existing case ('delivers a backlog of N within one poll interval') only asserts an UPPER bound on latency, so it passes more emphatically the faster the loop spins.
remediation: Assert the cadence directly: after `subscribe`, drive the internal clock (fake timers, or a spy wrapping `setTimeout` as `index.test.ts` already does for `setInterval`) and pin that consecutive ticks are scheduled at exactly `poll_interval_ms` when a tick returns fewer than POLL_BATCH rows, and at 0 when it returns exactly POLL_BATCH. A cheap observable alternative: count `selectAfterStmt.all` invocations over a fixed wall-clock window and assert `calls <= window/pollIntervalMs + slack` for two well-separated intervals.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a knob core/operators can set is validated but its effect is never measured'. Add a parameterized table in test/background-jobs.test.ts over `pollIntervalMs x rowsPending` — e.g. `[[MIN_POLL_INTERVAL_MS, 0], [50, 0], [200, 0], [200, POLL_BATCH], [1000, POLL_BATCH+1]]` — asserting BOTH a lower bound (ticks observed over a fixed window never exceed `window/interval + 1`, so ignoring the interval is red) and the existing upper bound (a full batch reschedules at 0). Widen it to cover the other accepted-but-unobserved knob, `retention_days`' PRUNE_INTERVAL_MS cadence, which is currently pinned only by the `setInterval` spy's `ms` argument and not by re-prune behaviour.

summary: MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS documents itself as load-bearing ('keep it at setTimeout's 32-bit limit: Node silently clamps a larger delay to 1 ms, so an operator asking for a very slow poll would get a hot loop instead'), yet no case pins the accept/reject edge. The only test that references the constant (`backoffMs(MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS, 11) === 30000`) passes for any large value, and config-validation's only over-ceiling probe is `1e308`. Contrast MAX_PAGE, whose boundary IS pinned at both `MAX_PAGE` and `MAX_PAGE + 1` — the right pattern exists in this same package and was not applied here.
failure: Mutation: `export const MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 2_147_483_647;` -> `1_099_511_627_776;`. Full package suite: `Tests 351 passed (351)`. Post-mutation, `backend_config: { poll_interval_ms: 3000000000 }` is accepted by `validateBackendConfig`, reaches `setTimeout(tick, 3e9)`, and Node emits TimeoutOverflowWarning and clamps the delay to 1 ms — the operator asked for a 35-day poll and got the hot loop the constant exists to prevent, with the bridge reporting a clean start.
remediation: Add the two edge rows to the config-validation table: `poll_interval_ms: MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` accepted, `MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS + 1` rejected with a message naming the ceiling; likewise `MIN_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` accepted / `MIN_POLL_INTERVAL_MS - 1` rejected.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a documented boundary constant is graded only from far outside it'. Make config-validation.test.ts derive its cases from the constants: for every bounded numeric key, generate `[min-1 reject, min accept, mid accept, max accept, max+1 reject]` from the exported constants rather than hand-picked literals, so any future re-tuning of MIN/MAX (or a new bounded key) is boundary-graded automatically — the shape `test/index.test.ts` already uses for MAX_PAGE.

summary: `readOrMintStoreId` accepts whatever string sits in `parley_meta.store_id` without checking it against the shape `parseCursor` demands (`/^[0-9a-f]{16}$/`). The plugin will then MINT cursors it immediately REJECTS as malformed: minting is unvalidated while parsing is strict, and nothing enforces that the two agree. `connect()` validates every operator-supplied knob before touching the file, but not this read-back value, which is the one input that decides whether the backend can honour its own cursors.
failure: Reproduced (probe run under vitest, since deleted): open a store, `UPDATE parley_meta SET value='AABBCCDDEEFF0011' WHERE key='store_id'` (uppercase hex — a perfectly reasonable variant), reconnect, `post()`, `fetchRecent({topic})` -> `nextCursor: 'AABBCCDDEEFF0011.1'`; feeding that cursor straight back -> `Error: parley-sqlite: malformed cursor 'AABBCCDDEEFF0011.1' for topic ctx — expected '<storeId>.<rowid>' minted by this backend`. Same for `''` ('.1'), `'legacy-store'`, and any value containing a dot. Per the README this is fatal, not degraded: catch-up-on-start propagates it, so the bridge exits non-zero on EVERY start and no amount of clearing read-state fixes it, because the plugin re-mints the same unparseable cursor. Reachable from a hand-edit, a restore/migration tool, a future Parley writing a different id format, or any peer with write access to the shared multi-session `.db` file — a one-statement permanent denial of service on every bridge sharing that store.
remediation: Validate the read-back at connect against the same pattern the parser uses, and fail fast naming `parley_meta.store_id` and the file (or, if you prefer self-healing, re-mint and rewrite it). Better: derive both `mintCursor` and `CURSOR_RE` from one exported STORE_ID_RE so the mint and parse sides cannot drift, and assert at connect that `parseCursor(mintCursor(storeId, 1n)) !== undefined`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'the plugin can produce an identifier its own parser rejects'. Add a parameterized case in test/cursor-replay.test.ts over planted `parley_meta.store_id` values — `['', 'legacy-store', 'AABBCCDDEEFF0011', 'de.adbeef', 'a'.repeat(64), '0123456789abcde' (15 chars)]` — asserting connect() either rejects naming the key, or every cursor the plugin mints round-trips through `fetchRecent({since})` without throwing. Complement it with a property case: for any store the plugin will connect to, `fetchRecent({topic, since: (await fetchRecent({topic})).nextCursor})` must never reject — the invariant 'a cursor this backend minted is always a cursor this backend accepts', which no current test states.

summary: README and driver.ts promise that a user with 'no prebuilt binary for your platform/ABI and no toolchain to build one' lands gracefully on the `node:sqlite` fallback, and test/driver-parity.test.ts grades that path in full. But `better-sqlite3` is a hard `dependencies` entry, and better-sqlite3@12 ships `"install": "prebuild-install || node-gyp rebuild --release"` — for a non-optional dependency npm treats a failing install script as fatal. The install aborts before a line of Parley code runs, so the very scenario the fallback is documented and tested for cannot be reached by installing this package.
failure: `npm install @sharptrick/parley-sqlite` on a platform/ABI with no better-sqlite3 prebuild and no C++ toolchain: `prebuild-install` fails, `node-gyp rebuild` fails, npm exits non-zero and installs nothing. The user never gets the README's 'the plugin code above the driver doesn't care which one is active' — they get a gyp build log. (The fallback IS still reachable via `ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED`, i.e. a Node major upgrade after a successful install, which is a different situation from the one the README names.)
remediation: Move `better-sqlite3` to `optionalDependencies` (npm continues past a failed optional install script, which is exactly this idiom), keep `@types/better-sqlite3` in devDependencies, and correct the README sentence to name the two triggers driver.ts actually handles: module absent (optional install skipped/failed) and ABI mismatch after a Node upgrade.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a documented degraded-mode path is unreachable through the shipped manifest'. Extend test/publish-hygiene.test.ts with a manifest-vs-code table: for every module driver.ts is willing to fall back FROM (parsed from the `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`/`ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED` branch, or listed in a small exported constant), assert it is declared in `optionalDependencies`, not `dependencies`. The same row shape then covers any future optional native driver without a new test.

summary: A RESP error is embedded verbatim in connect()'s failure message, so a server that echoes command arguments hands the URL's password straight back into the plugin's own error — which cli.ts writes to stderr. The plugin's own invariant (`endpointOf`: "never the password, which must not reach a log line") is defeated by the one string it does not control.
failure: `connect({ url: 'redis://:hunter2@host:6379' })` against a server that answers AUTH with Redis's own unknown-command wording (`-ERR unknown command 'AUTH', with args beginning with: 'hunter2', …` — what a real Redis returns when AUTH is renamed via `rename-command`, and what a RESP-speaking non-Redis service on a mis-pointed port returns) produces, reproduced verbatim in my worktree: `parley-redis: connected to 127.0.0.1:34765 but the server refused a command: ERR unknown command 'AUTH', with args beginning with: 'hunter2', 'CLIENT', 'SETINFO', …`. cli.ts then writes `err.stack` to stderr, i.e. the password lands in the operator's log/CI output. The README tells operators to put the password in the URL, so this is the documented deployment.
remediation: Redact before composing: parse the configured URL once at `open()`, keep its password, and strip every occurrence of it (and of the raw URL) from any server-supplied string before it reaches `refused()`, `labelled()` or `reportLiveDeliveryStopped()`. Better, drop the `with args beginning with:` tail entirely — keep only the RESP error code plus a bounded, redacted remainder.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "server-controlled text carries the credential back": add a `respondsWith` axis to `failure-modes.test.ts`'s degraded-server table whose replies ECHO the credential (real Redis unknown-command wording; a `WRONGPASS`/`NOPERM` variant that quotes the argument), and assert on EVERY surface a secret can escape through — thrown `message`, `stack`, and captured `process.stderr.write` calls — that the URL's password never appears, generated over every path that embeds server text (connect, post, fetchRecent, blocking fetchRecent, the subscribe stderr line), not just connect. The existing `expect(failure?.message).not.toContain('hunter2')` row is too narrow: it only catches the plugin composing the URL itself (I mutated `refused()` to interpolate `url` and it went red), never the server echoing it.

summary: Server-supplied RESP error text is embedded raw and unbounded into seam errors (which core renders as an `isError` tool result, i.e. model context) and into a stderr line, with no length bound and no control-character stripping — the exact class `bridge-net-util`'s `sanitizeBody` exists for and which every HTTP backend in this repo routes through.
failure: A server answering `-WRONGTYPE forged<ESC>[31m line<U+0085> AAAA…(5000 chars)` yields, reproduced: an Error whose `message` is 5105 chars and still contains U+001B and U+0085 (`has ESC: true has NEL: true`). Via `labelled()` on post/fetchRecent that string is rethrown by core's `parley_fetch_recent` handler and becomes model context; via `reportLiveDeliveryStopped()` it becomes an operator log line with forged line structure/ANSI. Nothing bounds either.
remediation: Route every server-supplied string through a sanitizer before it enters an Error or a stderr write: bound it (`MAX_ERROR_BODY`) and replace `\p{Cc}`/`\p{Cf}`/U+2028/U+2029 and lone surrogates — i.e. reuse `sanitizeBody` from `@sharptrick/parley-net-util` rather than restating a second policy here.
testUpgrade: One parameterized "hostile backend text" table (over-long body, ESC, U+0085 NEL, U+2028, a lone surrogate) × every surface that embeds server text (connect refusal, `labelled()` on post/fetchRecent/subscribe, the live-delivery-STOPPED stderr line), asserting a length ceiling and that no Cc/Cf codepoint survives. Today no case anywhere in the package feeds a RESP error the plugin did not itself shape, so the whole class is unguarded.

summary: The stale-cursor self-heal is only consulted once XRANGE has returned EMPTY, so a well-formed cursor that makes XRANGE itself fail never reaches the heal — it wedges the topic permanently, which is precisely what the heal exists to prevent.
failure: `fetchRecent({ topic, since: '18446744073709551615-18446744073709551615' })` on a live topic throws `parley-redis: ERR invalid start ID for the interval (topic …, key …)` (reproduced against redis:7-alpine; `XRANGE k (18446744073709551615-18446744073709551615 +` is refused because the exclusive start cannot be incremented). The immediate neighbours `18446744073709551615-0` and bare `18446744073709551615` both self-heal and return the recent window. Core's `catchUpTopic` rethrows anything that is not a NoSuchTopicError and never advances read-state, so this topic hits the same wall on every restart with no error the operator can act on — the same dead end the README promises cannot happen.
remediation: Decide staleness independently of the query: compare `since` against `lastGeneratedId` before issuing XRANGE when the cursor sits at the uint64 ceiling, or treat an `invalid start ID for the interval` refusal as the stale-cursor arm and fall into the heal.
testUpgrade: Widen the `shapes` generator in `live-failure-modes.test.ts`'s "a cursor past the high-water mark self-heals" block with boundary ids DERIVED from the uint64 ceiling (max-ms/max-seq, max-ms/max-seq-1, max-ms/0, bare max-ms) rather than one hand-picked constant — the existing row 'the largest id a stream can ever mint' samples the only ceiling value XRANGE happens to accept, so the class it names is not the class it grades. Same generator should assert the invariant "no well-formed cursor ever rejects" rather than the one heal outcome.

summary: The degraded-server table's in-process RESP fakes reply with hand-written, argument-free error strings (`-ERR unknown command`), while a real Redis always appends `, with args beginning with: '<arg>', …`. Every assertion built on those rows — including the "never the password" one — therefore grades a server that cannot produce the failure mode that matters.
failure: Row 'a non-Redis TCP speaker that answers the handshake' replies `-ERR unknown command\r\n`; with the real wording substituted (`-ERR unknown command 'AUTH', with args beginning with: 'hunter2', …`) the same code path leaks the credential into the error message and past `expect(failure?.message).not.toContain('hunter2')` — reproduced. The suite is green either way, so the credential-exposure guard is coverage that cannot fail against the realistic input.
remediation: Give the fake a reply builder that reproduces Redis's actual error grammar (code + quoted arguments) for the commands node-redis sends, and drive the degraded rows from it, so a row's wording is a property of the protocol rather than of what the test author typed.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the degraded-server table on (refusal code × whether the server echoes arguments), and assert the invariants that must hold on both arms: the message names the endpoint and the RESP code, never the credential, never more than the bound. A single generator also covers future codes (NOPROTO, EXECABORT) that PERMANENT_SERVER_ERROR lists but no row exercises.

summary: post() checks a client out of the shared pool BEFORE it blocks on `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, and no `lock_timeout`/`statement_timeout` is set. A lock wait therefore consumes pool capacity indefinitely: once `pool_size` posts to a contended topic are in flight, every read on the instance (fetchRecent, resolveIdentity, the subscribe drain) queues behind them forever, with no error and no diagnostic. README's "`pool_size` is safe to vary per session — it's per-instance capacity, not shared state" is misleading for the same reason.
failure: Reproduced against a real server (packages/bridge-postgres, throwaway pg on :5442). An outside session holds `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('locked-topic'))`. Then, on a plugin connected with `pool_size: 1`, `post('locked-topic', …)` is issued, followed 300ms later by `fetchRecent({topic:'locked-topic', since:'0'})`. Expected: the read (which needs no lock) returns. Actual: the read never resolves — still pending after 1.5s and unbounded thereafter. Repeated with the DEFAULT `pool_size: 5` and 5 concurrent posts: identical hang. The plugin is fully wedged for reads by a write-side lock wait; core's `parley_fetch_recent` has no timeout of its own, so the MCP call hangs until the client gives up.
remediation: Bound the wait and stop it consuming read capacity: issue `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '<n>s'` (or use `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock` with bounded retry) inside post()'s transaction so a wedged lock surfaces as a named `parley-postgres: …` error instead of an unbounded hang; and either give writes their own small pool or reserve read capacity so a blocked post cannot exhaust the pool shared with fetchRecent/drain. Correct the README's `pool_size` sentence to say the value is the head-of-line budget for writes as well as reads.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a seam call that blocks on a server-side lock must not consume the capacity other seam calls need": a parameterized real-server case over `pool_size` in {1, 2, 5} x blockedPosts in {1, pool_size, pool_size+1}, where an admin session holds `pg_advisory_lock(hashtext(topic))`, N posts are launched, and the assertion is that `fetchRecent` on the SAME and on a DIFFERENT topic still resolves within a bounded budget — and that the blocked post itself eventually rejects with a `parley-postgres:` message rather than hanging. Generalize the generator to any future site that takes a pooled client across a blocking server-side wait. No existing case covers this: connection-hygiene.test.ts races connect/disconnect but never contends the advisory lock, and cursor-loss/conformance only ever contend it between healthy writers that release promptly.

summary: The package guards every fire-and-forget path with a post-await `this.stopped || epoch !== this.epoch` re-check, and the suite grades most of them — but two are vacuous. Deleting them leaves all 580 tests green, so they are counted as covered while nothing would notice their removal.
failure: Two mutations, each run against the full package suite with a real server: (1) delete the post-`acquireListen` teardown check in `waitForNotify` (index.ts:518-522, the `releaseListen`+`return` block) -> 580 passed; (2) delete `if (this.stopped || this.pool === undefined || epoch !== this.epoch) return;` from prune()'s batch loop (index.ts:357) -> 580 passed. For contrast the same mutation applied at four other sites all failed loudly: adoptListener (2 failures), open()'s post-bootstrap guard (1), drain()'s post-query guard (6), startSubscription's registration order (4). Consequence of (1) if it ever regresses: a `fetchRecent` whose LISTEN landed just as `disconnect()` completed registers into the already-cleared `waiters`/`pendingAborts` maps, so no abort exists for it and the caller parks for the FULL `blockMs` (up to catchup.block_max_ms, 60s) past teardown while holding a LISTEN ref.
remediation: Extend the existing teardown-race table so it enumerates the await points rather than a hand-picked subset: drive `disconnect()` into the window after `acquireListen` resolves in `waitForNotify`, and into prune()'s inter-batch await, asserting the wait returns immediately and that no DELETE is issued after teardown / into a successor lifecycle.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "every await inside a background chore is a teardown/epoch boundary": a parameterized table with one row per await site — {open post-bootstrap, adoptListener, startSubscription post-LISTEN, waitForNotify post-LISTEN, drain post-query, prune inter-batch, reconnect post-connect} — each row forcing `disconnect()` (and, for the epoch half, a subsequent `connect()`) to land in that window and asserting (a) the chore stops, (b) nothing is delivered/deleted into the successor lifecycle, (c) no connection or LISTEN ref is left behind. Derive the row list from the source (e.g. count `epoch !== this.epoch` occurrences and pin the count by value, as suite-hygiene.test.ts already does for harness helpers) so a new guard site added later is a missing row, not silence.

summary: The 3x3 blackout table names the property "a seam call across a listener blackout never surfaces a raw driver error", but its only assertion of that property sits behind `if (rejection !== undefined)`. For 4 of the 9 cells the call cannot reject by construction, so those rows run for seconds and grade nothing.
failure: Mutated `listenerUnavailable` (index.ts:180) to `return err as Error;` — i.e. the raw node-postgres string escapes the seam, exactly the defect the file exists to catch. Result: only 2 of 9 cells failed (`subscribe a new topic` x the two blackout windows). The 4 blackout cells for `blocking fetchRecent` and `subscribe the same topic again` passed, because `waitForNotify` swallows the listener error and returns, and a repeat subscribe takes the `this.subs.get(channel)` fast path without touching the listener — so `rejection` is undefined and the assertion body is skipped. The 3 `after the reconnect has landed` cells assert a different (real) property. Net: 4 rows cost ~1.2s each and cannot fail.
remediation: Split the file's two properties and make each cell assert unconditionally: for calls that MUST reject in the blackout, assert a rejection whose message starts with `parley-postgres:` and names the topic; for calls that MUST succeed (repeat subscribe, blocking fetch degrading to core's poll fallback), assert the success AND the observable consequence (the fetch returned an empty page within its budget; the repeat subscribe's handler receives a message once the reconnect lands) rather than merely not throwing.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a table row whose assertion is behind an `if` can silently grade nothing": give each cell an explicit `expects: 'rejects' | 'resolves'` field and assert that outcome unconditionally, so a cell that changes arm fails instead of passing quietly. Add a suite-hygiene rule alongside the existing ones in test/suite-hygiene.test.ts banning `expect(` nested under an `if (…!== undefined)` inside an `it.each` body, and re-run the `listenerUnavailable` pass-through mutation as the acceptance check — all blackout cells must fail.

summary: Both the published README and prune()'s JSDoc justify PRUNE_BATCH with a lock-contention mechanism PostgreSQL does not have: they claim an unbatched retention DELETE would make every `post()` queue behind it. Deleting old rows never blocks inserting new ones under MVCC, and prune takes no advisory lock, so the stated reason is false. Batching is still good practice — the reason given for it is not, and an operator sizing retention from this text is reasoning from a wrong model.
failure: Reproduced on postgres:16-alpine: session A runs `BEGIN; DELETE FROM lt WHERE ts < '2030-01-01';` over 50 000 rows and holds the transaction open (pg_sleep 8). Session B then runs `INSERT INTO lt(topic,ts) VALUES ('t','2031-01-01');` — it completes in 3.174 ms, not blocked at all. README.md:58-61 says "in batches of 5000 rows per statement, so the first prune ... cannot become one long DELETE that every `post()` queues behind", and src/index.ts:346-348 says the same ("one long DELETE holding row locks while every advisory-lock-serialized `post()` queues behind it").
remediation: State the real reasons for batching (bounded transaction size/WAL, not pinning a long-running snapshot against autovacuum, incremental progress across restarts) or drop the rationale entirely — per CLAUDE.md, why-this-approach belongs in the commit message. Remove the `post()`-queues-behind claim from README.md and from prune()'s JSDoc.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a published doc claim about backend concurrency semantics that no test exercises": add a real-server case per such claim, asserting the behaviour rather than the prose — here, that a `post()` completes within a small budget while a full-table retention DELETE is deliberately in flight (parameterized over backlog sizes either side of PRUNE_BATCH, and over same-topic vs other-topic). A claim that cannot be written as such a case is the signal to delete the claim.

summary: `retention_days` is validated only as "a finite number > 0", with an error message asserting that 0/negative are refused because they "would delete the whole history". Both ends of the accepted range defeat that reasoning: a value just above 0 deletes the whole history, and a very large value silently disables pruning entirely — a validated knob that becomes a no-op with no error anywhere.
failure: Destructive end: `retention_days: 1e-9` passes validateBackendConfig, yielding a cutoff ~0.09 ms in the past, so the connect-time prune deletes essentially all history — the exact outcome the rejection message for `0` claims to be preventing (the package's own retention.test.ts uses 1/86_400_000 for precisely this effect). Silent-no-op end: `retention_days: 1e12` passes validation; prune() computes `new Date(Date.now() - 1e12 * 86_400_000)` = Invalid Date, `.toISOString()` throws RangeError, and the deliberately-broad `catch {}` at index.ts:366 swallows it — so pruning never runs, forever, while README.md:58 tells the operator rows are "deleted on connect and hourly thereafter". Verified: node reports `RangeError: Invalid time value` for that expression, and 1e8 days yields the year `-271765`, whose ISO text sorts below every stored `ts` so `ts < $1` matches nothing.
remediation: Bound the knob to a window whose cutoff is representable and whose effect is what an operator would predict — reject anything whose computed cutoff is not a valid Date, and reject (or at minimum refuse to act on) sub-second windows, with the message naming the computed cutoff. Alternatively make prune() distinguish a transient query failure from an un-computable cutoff and fail connect() on the latter rather than swallowing it.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "an operator-supplied numeric knob accepted at a magnitude where it silently does nothing or does the opposite of its stated purpose": widen config-validation.test.ts into a boundary generator over {just below the floor, the floor, just above the floor, a nominal value, just below the ceiling, the ceiling, just above the ceiling, Number.MAX_VALUE, 1e-9, denormal} for every numeric key (`retention_days`, `pool_size`), asserting for each that it is either rejected by name OR produces the documented observable effect against a real table — never accepted-and-inert. Today's table only walks pool_size's integer bounds and retention_days' sign.

summary: `ensureListener()` memoizes the listener Client and neither the `error` nor the `end` handler clears `listenerPromise`. For the whole reconnect blackout, every caller is handed the CLOSED client, so `subscribe()` on a not-yet-subscribed topic is guaranteed to fail rather than wait for the reconnect the plugin already has in flight — and core's push loop rethrows anything that is not a NoSuchTopicError, so the bridge fails to come up.
failure: Traced end to end and exercised by the package's own listener-blackout suite: with topic A already subscribed, killing the listener ('end' with the client marked dead) makes `subscribe(B)` reject with `parley-postgres: could not establish the live path for topic 'B' … a reconnect is in flight, so a retry succeeds once it lands` — but nobody retries. packages/bridge-core/src/transport/push-loop.ts:66-72 rethrows non-NoSuchTopicError out of `startPushLoop`, so `createStdioBridge` rejects and packages/bridge-postgres/src/cli.ts:53 exits(1). Concrete input: a config with topics [A, B] where the database restarts (or an admin terminates the backend) between the two subscribes -> the bridge dies instead of coming up ~500ms later.
remediation: Make the listener memo reflect reality: clear `listenerPromise` when the connection ends, and have `ensureListener()` await the in-flight reconnect (bounded) instead of returning a dead client — so a subscribe issued during the blackout blocks briefly and then succeeds, and only a reconnect that exhausts its budget rejects. The error text already promises this behaviour; the code should provide it rather than describe it.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a memoized connection outlives its socket and is handed to a later caller": a parameterized case per seam entry point that touches the listener ({subscribe new topic, subscribe existing topic, blocking fetchRecent}) x per blackout phase ({connection ended, reconnect attempt failing, reconnect landed}), asserting the call SUCCEEDS once the reconnect lands within a bounded budget and that its live path actually delivers a subsequently-posted message — not merely that the error string was well-formed, which is all today's table asks.

summary: The prime directive holds mechanically — bridge-core imports no backend, and bridge-postgres imports only the public `@sharptrick/parley-core` surface — but core's `safeName` JSDoc pins its own behaviour to a named plugin: "Hash is over the RAW topic's UTF-8 bytes, exactly like bridge-postgres channelFor." That is a one-way dependency drawn in prose, and it is already inaccurate.
failure: Read both sides: core's safeName uses `createHash('sha1')` with a 10-char truncation, while bridge-postgres `channelFor` (src/schema.ts:123) uses full `createHash('md5')` and does not call safeName at all — postgres never imports the helper the comment claims parity with. A future change to either side reads as if it must preserve agreement with the other, which is exactly the "special-case a backend inside core" pressure CLAUDE.md forbids; and today the sentence tells a reader the two derivations match when only the input encoding does.
remediation: State the invariant without naming a backend — e.g. "the digest is taken over the topic's raw UTF-8 bytes, not a sanitized form" — and, if parity with a plugin's channel derivation is genuinely required, express it as a shared exported helper the plugin calls rather than as a comment in core.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "core naming a specific backend": extend the existing source-hygiene rule in packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts to fail on any occurrence of a backend package/dir name (`bridge-<x>` / `parley-<x>` for every directory under packages/ except core, net-util and conformance) anywhere in bridge-core's non-test sources — comments included — with the plugin list read from the filesystem so a backend added later is covered automatically. Allow only config.ts's deliberate binary-name hint, pinned by value.

summary: `validateConfig` bounds `sync_timeout_ms` only below (positive integer). Any value above ~2_147_453_647 makes `syncDeadlineMs(t) = t + 30000` exceed 2^31-1, which Node's timer clamps to 1ms — so every `/sync` aborts client-side after 1ms, the live path dies, and the operator's stderr blames the homeserver. The README's config table and the `syncDeadlineMs` JSDoc both claim the opposite ("Unbounded above … so raising it does not make the homeserver's own answer look like a timeout").
failure: Against the live Synapse in examples/dev-compose: `backend_config: { sync_timeout_ms: 3000000000 }` (accepted at load) → `subscribe()` + `post()` delivers NOTHING in 5s; stderr repeats `[parley-matrix] /sync failed … deadline: no response within 3000030000` (it actually aborted at 1ms). The identical run at 25000 delivers the message. Reproduced; the accepted-value table in config-validation.test.ts only tries 1 / 25_000 / 60_000.
remediation: Give `sync_timeout_ms` an upper bound in `validateConfig` derived from the timer it feeds — reject anything where `syncDeadlineMs(t) > 2 ** 31 - 1`, naming the ceiling — the same way `0`/`NaN`/`Infinity` are refused. Then correct the README row and the `syncDeadlineMs` JSDoc, which currently promise "unbounded above".
testUpgrade: Parameterize the CLASS "a timing knob whose legal-but-extreme value collapses the path it configures" over BOTH ends of the range, not just the low end that `park-rate.fake.test.ts` already sweeps: add `sync_timeout_ms` rows at `2**31 - 1 - DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS`, `+1` past it, and `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` to `config-validation.test.ts`'s accepted/rejected table, and add a live-or-fake case asserting that every accepted value still yields a delivered live message (i.e. no accepted value may produce a `/sync` deadline error). Generalize the generator to any plugin knob that is fed to `setTimeout`/`AbortSignal.timeout`.

summary: `configRisks` warns about the default password, `shared_room` and `public_chat`, but says nothing when `homeserver_url` is `http://` to a NON-loopback host — even though `connect()` then POSTs `m.login.password` with the operator's real secret in the clear and carries the resulting bearer `access_token` on every subsequent request. summary: onPresence attributes a `<presence type='error'>` to whatever join is currently pending on that room WITHOUT checking the occupant nick it names — the exact guard the success path applies three lines later — so a superseded join's error rejects the innocent successor and can silently downgrade the connection's occupant nick.

Result: `subscribe` REJECTS with `MUC join error (forbidden) for t-…@muc.parley.local` while the successor join for `ctx-payments` succeeds and a subsequent `post` returns `arch-1`. A subscribe rejection is what `startPushLoop` rethrows, so a reconnect/nick-adoption landing during startup takes the bridge process down for a room it is in. (b) Same shape with `conflictNicks = {provisionalNick}` only (the handle `ctx-payments` is FREE): the conflict presence for the provisional nick rejects the `ctx-payments` entry, `doJoin` calls revertToProvisionalNick, `post` rejects with `MUC join error (conflict)` and `priv(plugin).nick` is permanently the random `parley-7a80e3…` — the operator sees `parley_list_users` report a random name and a stderr line saying `could not take 'ctx-payments' … another occupant holds it`, which is false.
remediation: Apply the same attribution rule to the error arm as to the self-presence arm: in `onPresence`, take `pending` only when `resourceOf(from)` is `''` or equals `pending.nick` (a service rewrite cannot appear on an error), otherwise drop the stanza. While there, tighten the sibling fall-through in `onErrorMessage` (line 757): a `<message type='error'>` carrying no id currently rejects whatever join is pending on the room, which is the same class one stanza kind over.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a stanza naming an occupant nick this connection did not ask for settles or fails a keyed operation". In `correlator-provenance.test.ts` the stray-join stanza is hard-coded to `presenceError(room)` built from `OUR_NICK`, so the class has no row at all — parameterize it over a nick axis {the pending join's own nick, a superseded previous nick, another occupant's nick, no resource at all} crossed with presence type {error, available} and status set {none, 110, 110+210}, asserting that only the first nick (or an explicit 210) may settle/fail the join, with the legitimate stanza as the negative control in each row. Add a `superseded join answered with an error` trigger to `join-supersession.test.ts`'s trigger table (it only ever answers the superseded join successfully), parameterized over conditions {forbidden, conflict, registration-required, item-not-found}, demanding the original caller still completes.

summary: A since-less `fetchRecent` returns the NEWEST `limit` messages, but a since-less `fetchRecent` WITH `blockMs` that has to park returns the OLDEST `limit` — the same call answers a different window depending on whether the topic happened to be idle at the moment it was issued.
failure: Reproduced with FakeXmpp. Non-blocking: archive `m0..m4`, `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 2})` → `['m3','m4']` (the conformance clause 'a since-less fetch returns the NEWEST messages, not the oldest'). Blocking: empty archive, `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 2, blockMs: 1000})`, then 6 messages `n0..n5` land 60 ms in → `['n0','n1']`, nextCursor `arch-2`. The since-less arm falls through to `blockingMam(topic, since ?? '', …)`, which runs `exclusiveMam` from the ZERO cursor — 'from the very beginning' — instead of re-taking the last-page window. Core's `fetchRecentBlocking` issues exactly this call (`since: undefined`, `blockMs: remaining`) for every `parley_fetch_recent` from an agent that holds no cursor, so it is the hot path, not a corner. Nothing is lost (the cursor is coherent), but an agent asking to be caught up on the newest gets the oldest of the burst, and no other backend behaves this way. The blockMs arm-table in `long-poll-wake.test.ts` only ever delivers ONE message during the block, so it cannot see the direction.
remediation: In `blockingMam`, when the caller supplied no `since`, re-run the since-LESS window (`mamQuery({before: true, max: limit})`) on each iteration rather than `exclusiveMam(topic, '', limit)`, so the direction the since-less contract states holds on both arms. Alternatively document the divergence in the README's block_ms paragraph — but silently swapping window direction on an argument that is only a latency hint is the astonishing option.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "an optional argument that changes which window a read returns, not just when it returns". Widen the `armCells` table in `long-poll-wake.test.ts` with a `burst` axis (1 message vs `limit + 3` messages arriving during the block) and assert, for every since-arm × history × mode cell, that the returned contents equal what the SAME cell returns with `blockMs: 0` once the messages are already present — i.e. blockMs may change latency and nothing else. Add the corresponding clause to `packages/conformance` so every backend is graded on it (`a since-less blocking fetch returns the same window as a since-less fetch`).

summary: `resolveIdentity` returns `backendRef === handle`, but the backend-native reference this handle actually produces is `nickFor(handle)` — the folded, hash-disambiguated MUC nick — so the seam reports an identifier that will never appear as a `senderHandle` whenever the fold is lossy.

Posting under the same handle archives (and reads back) as `alice_corp.com-<10-hex>` because `nickFor` runs `safeName(…, sanitizeNick)` (index.ts:1311) — `@` is not in the resource charset, so the fold is lossy and a disambiguating suffix is appended. seam.ts:39 defines `backendRef` as "a provisioned Matrix user / XMPP JID …", i.e. the backend-native name; an operator resolving an identity to debug why `@alice@corp.com` does not match anything in `parley_list_users` is handed the string that does NOT match rather than the one that does.

Parameterize `name-folds.test.ts`'s handle table (it already crosses length × charset, including lossy handles) with an assertion that `resolveIdentity(h).backendRef` equals the `senderHandle` a real `post(topic, h, …)` reads back for that same handle — one property over the existing generator, which catches every future divergence between the fold and the accessor, not just the `@` case.

summary: Catch-up detects a re-provisioned stream only while the new incarnation is SHORTER than the persisted cursor; once it grows past that sequence the plugin silently skips every message below it.
failure: Stream re-created out-of-band; core's persisted cursor is "500" from the old incarnation; the new incarnation already holds 600 messages (n1..n600). `fetchRecent({topic, since: '500', limit: 1000})` → `restarted = since > lastSeq` is `500 > 600` = false, so `startSeq = 501` and the page returns n501..n600 with nextCursor 600. n1..n500 are never returned by any later call — reproduced: `expected [ 'n501', … ] to include 'n1'`. `subscribe` compares `info.created` and so does notice, but it only resumes at the new tail, so it does not backfill them either. The README and msg-id.test.ts both assert the opposite ("catch-up already falls back to the retained window" / "restarting it is what the catch-up fallback already handles").
remediation: Qualify the cursor with the same incarnation token `backendMsgId` already carries: mint `nextCursor` as `<incarnation>-<seq>` and have `parseCursor` split it (accepting a bare decimal as the legacy form). `readRecent` then decides `restarted` by comparing the cursor's incarnation to `info.created`, which is exact and independent of how far the new stream has grown. The cursor is opaque to core (bridge-core/src/message.ts), so this needs no core change.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the re-provision table in test/cursor-input.test.ts over the new incarnation's LENGTH relative to the persisted cursor — shorter, equal, longer, and much longer — with the fake's `streamCreated` swapped in each row, asserting that draining from the stale cursor yields the new incarnation's history in full. The existing `staleCursors = ['4','9','1000','9007199254740991']` rows only ever exercise cursors ABOVE the new tail, which is the one case that already works; test/subscribe-loop.test.ts's 'tails' table has exactly the right three-way shape and should be mirrored onto the catch-up path.

summary: The fake decides which records a consumer sees from its own `foreign` flag and never reads the `filter_subject` it is handed, so the whole foreign-publisher table certifies a property the plugin is not actually tested to have.

Against a real server the same mutant leaks: with the pre-existing wildcard stream that config.test.ts explicitly certifies as accepted (stream `PZ2_win`, subjects `['pz2.>']`, subject_prefix `pz2.`), `subscribe(topic 'win')` delivered a message published to `pz2.secret-other-topic` into the handler — an un-allowlisted subject reaching agent context, which is exactly what CLAUDE.md's 'inbound is untrusted / respect the topic allowlist' rule forbids. No live test catches it either, because every live file uses a per-run subject_prefix/stream_prefix so each stream captures exactly one topic and `filter_subject` is a no-op.

Add one live case that stands up a shared wildcard stream and asserts neither `fetchRecent` nor `subscribe` returns a message from a sibling subject.
