Give fake-jetstream.ts a self-fidelity describe (like the existing 'nats pull fake fidelity' block) that asserts the fake's own consumer honours `filter_subject`, `opt_start_seq` and `max_messages` as stated — a fake property test that fails if the shortcut returns. Then parameterize a shared-wildcard-stream case over {catch-up, long-poll, subscribe} × {sibling subject, deeper subject, exact subject} so any path that forgets the filter fails on the axis it forgot.

summary: When the newest `limit` sequences hold none of the topic's own messages, the since-less read widens to the entire retained range in one pull and materializes every message in the topic's history to return `limit` of them.
failure: Real server, stream `PZ_win` with subjects `['pz.>']`, 50 000 topic messages of ~400 bytes plus a 50-message foreign tail, the topic's newest message deleted so `last_by_subj` 404s: `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 5})` issues one `fetch({max_messages: 50050})`, the server streams all 49 999 surviving messages, and `pull` builds a 49 999-element `Message[]` before `read.slice(-5)` throws it away — 1107 ms and +34.9 MB heap for a five-message page, linear in history (≈1 M messages ⇒ ~700 MB, ~20 s). Core's cold start issues exactly this since-less call, and the same shape is repeated on every poll while the condition holds. `limit` (capped server-side at 1000 by core) bounds nothing here.
remediation: Bound both halves. In `pull`, keep only the newest `want`/`limit` messages (a ring buffer or `messages.splice(0, messages.length - keep)`) instead of accumulating the whole range; and instead of one full-range pull, walk backwards in windows of a bounded size from `tailSeq` toward `firstSeq`, stopping as soon as `limit` messages are held. That preserves the 'a deep hole must not strand the page' property the current single-shot widening was written for, without making the work proportional to the retained history.
testUpgrade: Class: 'work proportional to history rather than to `limit`'. Add a table over history depth × top-window hole depth (e.g. depth ∈ {10, 500, 5000} × hole ∈ {limit, 4×limit}) that asserts a bound on the fake's observed `max_messages` and on the number of records the fake actually yielded, not just on the page contents. test/window.test.ts's 'a deleted tail longer than any widening budget' row and prefix-live.test.ts's 'a since-less page returns the newest messages when the top sequences are deleted' both drive this exact path today and assert only the page, so they certify the behaviour without seeing its cost.

summary: The `configKeys` rows assert `readme.toContain(key)` against the whole README, so most of them pass on unrelated prose and cannot fail on the drift they exist to catch.
failure: Deleting all five documented auth fields (`token`, `user`, `pass`, `creds_file`, `nkey_seed`) from the README's `backend_config` block leaves docs.test.ts failing on ONE row: `user`. `token` still matches 'NATS subject tokens' and 'token cost'; `pass` matches 'is passed through'; `creds_file` and `nkey_seed` match the prose sentence '`creds_file` wins over `nkey_seed`'. An operator reading a README that no longer documents token or user/password auth would be told by a green suite that it does.
remediation: Assert the field is documented where a reader would use it: match `^\s*<key>:` inside the fenced `backend_config` YAML block (extract the block first), and derive the key list from the exported `NatsBackendConfig` interface rather than hard-coding it, so a new config field is undocumented-by-default rather than silently unpoliced.
testUpgrade: Class: 'documentation assertion satisfied by text other than the documentation'. Add a self-test row alongside the existing 'the banned-claim check reads a claim and spares its negation' meta-case: feed the checker a README with the config block stripped and assert every key row fails. Generalize the key list from the source interface so the table cannot drift behind the code.

summary: `if (lastSeq > info.state.last_seq) lastSeq = info.state.last_seq;` in the subscribe rebuild is unreachable given the `info.created !== created` reset two lines above, and deleting it leaves the whole suite green.
failure: Removing the line entirely: 11 files / 444 tests still pass. The only way a stream's `last_seq` moves backwards is a re-provision, which changes `created` and is already handled by the reset to `lastSeq = 0` immediately above; `nats stream purge` keeps `last_seq`. A reader has to reason about a case that cannot occur, and (as msg-id.test.ts's own comment says) the clamp 'looks like it covers' the re-provision case while covering nothing.
remediation: Delete the clamp. If it is being kept as a guard against a server that reports a lower `last_seq` without a new `created`, that is a distinct hypothesis and should be stated as a test rather than as an unreachable line — `opt_start_seq` above the tail is legal in JetStream anyway, so the clamp changes no outcome.
testUpgrade: Class: 'defensive branch no input can reach'. The durable guard is mutation coverage rather than another case: add the nats package to a mutation-testing run (Stryker or a scripted equivalent over src/index.ts) with a survivor budget of zero for statement deletions, so an unreachable branch is reported as an unkilled mutant instead of counting as covered code.

summary: `captures()`'s single-token `*` arm — the check that decides whether a pre-existing stream really covers this topic's subject — is exercised by no test, and neither is `pull`'s `m.seq >= tailSeq` early break.
failure: Mutating `if (tokens[i] !== '*' && tokens[i] !== target[i]) return false;` to `if (tokens[i] !== target[i]) return false;` leaves 444 tests green; the only wildcard case in config.test.ts uses `parley.>`. A wrong `*` arm makes the plugin refuse a legitimate pre-existing `parley.*` stream with a spurious 'differs from the instance that created it' error, or (in the opposite direction) accept a stream that does not capture the subject and then read an always-empty topic. Separately, deleting the `|| m.seq >= tailSeq` term from `pull`'s break also stays green (the suite merely runs ~15 s slower), so the documented 'a page ends at the topic tail' bound is unpinned and only the 200 ms idle close keeps reads prompt.
remediation: Unit-test `captures()` directly as a table over (pattern, subject) pairs covering `*` at head/middle/tail, `>` at tail, arity mismatch and exact match; and add a window row asserting the pull STOPPED at `tailSeq` (e.g. the fake records the number of records it was asked past the tail, or the elapsed time stays below the idle threshold rather than below expiry/2).
testUpgrade: Class: 'a decision function reachable only through a rarely-configured path'. Export `captures` (or test it via the plugin's private handle as docs.test.ts already does for `subject`/`streamName`) and drive it from a generator: random legal subjects × patterns built by replacing a random token with `*` or truncating with `>`, asserting agreement with a reference matcher. That covers arities and positions no hand-picked pair reaches, and would also catch a future prefix change that alters token counts.

summary: `connect()` half-implements re-entrancy: it bumps `generation`, resets `stopped`/`teardown` and clears `claimedWireTopics`, but leaves `waiters`, `queues`, `controllers`, `loopExits` and `pendingAborts` holding the previous connection's state — so a blocking fetchRecent parks its whole budget behind an orphaned loop that can never wake it, and the old connection's event queue leaks.
failure: Reproduced. connect(serverA) -> subscribe('orphan') (loop parks in a 30s long-poll on A) -> connect(serverB) with no disconnect -> post 'seed' on B, take the tail -> fetchRecent({topic:'orphan', since:tail, blockMs:4000}) while 'late' is posted at t+200ms. Observed: ELAPSED 4005ms (the entire budget) instead of ~200ms, and `registers on B: 0` — armWake saw the stale waiters entry with healthy>0 and piggybacked on the dead loop instead of opening its own queue. In the shipped product this is `parley_fetch_recent` with core's default catchup.block_max_ms=60000 returning empty after a full 60s while the message was already durable. Same run: DELETEs on A = 0, DELETEs on B = 1 — A's event queue is never released (it survives until Zulip's ~10min GC, against the bot's queue budget) and its opaque queue_id is disclosed to the unrelated server B.
remediation: Either make `connect()` reject when `this.connected` is already true (fail-fast, and the seam has no documented reconnect-in-place), or make it perform the same registry reset `disconnect()` does. The cleanest form is to factor the teardown of the per-connection registries out of `disconnect()` into a private `resetConnectionState()` and call it from both, so a registry added later cannot be reset in one path and forgotten in the other. If in-place reconnect is kept, the old queues must be deleted against the OLD baseUrl before it is overwritten.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any per-connection registry must be empty at the start of every connection, on every entry path. Add a parameterized table in subscription-lifecycle.test.ts crossing {teardown: disconnect-then-connect, connect-without-disconnect} x {same server, different server} x {parked in the long-poll, parked in failure backoff, parked in a gap-fill} and assert, for each cell, (i) a blocking fetchRecent on the subscribed topic wakes within a prompt bound rather than spending its budget, (ii) `requestCount('POST /api/v1/register')` on the new server is >0 when no live loop should exist there, and (iii) `requestCount('DELETE /api/v1/events')` on the OLD fake is >= its register count. The existing blocking-fetch.test.ts LOOP_STATES table already encodes 'never park behind a loop that cannot wake you' but never crosses a reconnect, which is exactly how this class walked around it; the existing 'disconnect then connect again' row in subscription-lifecycle.test.ts always disconnects first, so it cannot reach the connect-only path.

summary: The fake advertises itself as "a semantic MODEL of the REST API, not a permissive echo" and models the server's TOPIC rewrites (60-char truncation, case folding) in SERVER_CONSTRAINTS, but its write path stores `form.get('content')` verbatim — it models none of Zulip's documented body constraints — so every content-fidelity clause the shared conformance suite grades against this backend is graded against an echo.
failure: Demonstrated by mutation. Zulip's `zerver/lib/message.py::normalize_body` rewrites an accepted body (`body.rstrip().lstrip('\n')`, rejects empty and NUL, and caps at MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH=10000). Adding just the rstrip to the fake's POST /api/v1/messages and running `vitest run packages/bridge-zulip/test/conformance.test.ts -t "round-trips"` turns the frozen clause red: `post either round-trips leading and trailing spaces exactly or refuses it` -> AssertionError: expected '  fidelity' to be '  fidelity  ' (packages/conformance/src/index.ts:326). The plugin takes neither arm the clause permits — it does not preserve the payload and it does not refuse it. The same gap hides the sharper hazard: a `parley_post` of a 15000-character context hand-off (Parley's primary payload) is accepted, returns a successful id, and is silently stored truncated; nothing in the plugin, the fake, SERVER_CONSTRAINTS or the README mentions a message-size limit at all (`grep -i 'MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH|10000|message length'` across the package returns nothing).
remediation: Extend SERVER_CONSTRAINTS with the body constraints (maxMessageLength: 10000, the truncation marker, the rstrip/lstrip normalization, the empty and NUL rejections) and enforce them in the fake's POST /api/v1/messages, exactly as maxTopicNameLength is enforced today. Then make the plugin take one of the two arms the seam permits — the wireTopic precedent says refuse: reject a body that cannot survive the round trip at `post()`, naming the measured length, rather than letting the server silently rewrite an agent hand-off.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every server-side rewrite of a WRITE the plugin issues must be modelled by the fake and guarded by a plugin case — the topic path already is, the body path is not. Parameterize a `WRITE_REWRITES` table keyed by SERVER_CONSTRAINTS (topic length, topic case, body length, body whitespace normalization, forbidden code points), each row asserting post -> fetchRecent either returns the exact payload or `post` rejects naming the constraint, and add a self-test that every key of SERVER_CONSTRAINTS has a row so a constraint added to the table cannot sit ungraded. Widen the conformance content generator beyond its five fixed strings to include a trailing-whitespace/leading-newline generator and a length generator straddling each backend's stated cap.

summary: `connect()` reads five known keys off `backend_config` and silently ignores every other key, so a typo is a silent no-op — and for `api_key` the silent fallback is the world-known default credential. bridge-redis, bridge-sqlite and bridge-xmpp all reject unknown keys (`assertKnownKeys`, "Keep an unknown key a load error"); zulip is the outlier.
failure: Reproduced: `await new ZulipPlugin().connect({ site_url: 'https://z.example.com', email: 'bot@x', api_kye: 'REAL-SECRET', events_timeout: 60000 })` resolves successfully. The plugin then authenticates every request with the built-in `parley-api-key` against a real remote server, and runs a 25s poll cap the operator believed they had set to 60s. The only signal is the generic default-key SECURITY warning, which an operator who believes they set `api_key` will read as noise rather than as "your key was never read". Compare packages/bridge-redis/src/index.ts:208-212, which throws `parley-redis: unknown backend_config key '<key>' — expected one of ...`.
remediation: Add an `assertKnownKeys` to `connect()` derived from the declared `ZulipBackendConfig` key set, throwing before any other validation and naming both the offending key and the accepted set — the same shape bridge-redis/bridge-sqlite/bridge-xmpp already use. Keep it a load error; a lenient variant reintroduces exactly the silent fallback above.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no backend may accept a backend_config key it does not implement. Put this in the shared conformance/factory surface rather than per package: a table over every plugin asserting `connect({...validConfig, <unknownKey>: 'x'})` rejects naming the key, generated from each plugin's declared config interface (secret-hygiene.test.ts already parses `ZulipBackendConfig` out of the source, so the key set is available without hand-listing). Add a near-miss generator over the declared keys — a dropped character, a transposed pair, a snake/camel swap — so the row set widens with the config surface instead of pinning one typo.

summary: The same four server-fault literals are restated as inline object literals in four different test files instead of living beside the fake that serves them, so the files can drift apart on what "the same fault" means while every one of them stays green.
failure: `failRoute('GET /api/v1/events', { status: 500 })` appears in blocking-fetch.test.ts (LOOP_STATES row and DEGRADATIONS row), operability.test.ts (PERMANENT_FAILURES), and subscription-lifecycle.test.ts (PARK_POINTS). The BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID body is written out longhand in blocking-fetch.test.ts:213-216 and again as `BAD_QUEUE` in operability.test.ts:13-16. The empty-body fault `{ status: 200, body: { result: 'success' } }` appears in blocking-fetch.test.ts twice and operability.test.ts once, and push-loop-containment.test.ts carries a near-neighbour `{}`. Concretely: correcting the BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID shape (say, adding the `queue_id` field the real server sends, which the fake's own `badQueue` helper does send) in one file leaves the other grading a body the server never produces, and nothing goes red. harness.ts already exists as "the ONE fixture every zulip test file boots from" — the fault vocabulary is the obvious next thing it should own, and it does not.
remediation: Export a named fault vocabulary from test/fake-zulip.ts (which owns the wire shapes) or test/harness.ts — e.g. `FAULTS.eventsServerError`, `FAULTS.staleQueue`, `FAULTS.eventsEmptyBody`, `FAULTS.eventsBlackHole` — and have every table reference those names. Add a self-test asserting no test file contains an inline `failRoute(...)/hangRoute(...)` literal outside the vocabulary, the same way conformance.test.ts already lints for inline capability declarations.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a wire-shape literal restated in more than one test file is drift waiting to happen. Add a source lint (the package already uses this technique in conformance.test.ts:186-195, secret-hygiene.test.ts and comment-hygiene.test.ts) that scans every `test/*.test.ts`, extracts `failRoute`/`hangRoute`/`rateLimit`/`holdResponse` argument literals, and fails when a shape occurs in two files without coming from the shared vocabulary — so the check widens automatically as fault shapes are added, rather than pinning today's four.

summary: The gateway `message` listener dereferences `payload.d` without checking it, in a `ws` event handler that has no exception boundary. A single malformed frame raises an uncaught TypeError and kills the whole MCP server process — the REST half, every other topic, and core's catch-up with it.
failure: Reproduced against the compiled plugin and a real `ws` WebSocketServer (not the fake): a gateway that sends `{"op":10}` (HELLO with no `d`) → `UNCAUGHT: TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'heartbeat_interval')`, process exits. A gateway that sends `{"op":0,"t":"MESSAGE_CREATE","s":2,"d":null}` after READY → `UNCAUGHT: TypeError Cannot read properties of null (reading 'channel_id')` at line 880, process exits. `ws.on('error')` does not cover throws inside the `message` listener, and cli.ts installs no `uncaughtException` handler. Reachable from a `gateway_url` override (a documented config knob), any websocket intermediary, or a provider-side regression. The rest of the handler is deliberately hardened — non-JSON is swallowed, a throwing subscriber handler is caught, terminal close codes are classified — so this is a hole in an existing boundary, not an absent one.
remediation: Type-guard `payload.d` before use: in OP.HELLO require `typeof d?.heartbeat_interval === 'number'` and treat anything else as a protocol violation (close the socket and let the ladder retry) rather than dereferencing; in OP.DISPATCH require `typeof d?.channel_id === 'string'` before the `subs`/`waiters` lookups. Simplest durable form: wrap the whole `switch` body in the same try/catch the subscriber-handler call already has, so no future opcode branch can crash the process either.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any gateway frame whose `d` is missing, null, or the wrong shape must not escape the message listener. Add a table-driven suite parameterized over (opcode × malformed `d`) — `{op:10}`, `{op:10,d:null}`, `{op:10,d:{}}`, `{op:10,d:{heartbeat_interval:'x'}}`, `{op:0,t:'READY',d:null}`, `{op:0,t:'MESSAGE_CREATE',d:null}`, `{op:0,t:'MESSAGE_CREATE',d:{}}`, `{op:0,t:'MESSAGE_CREATE',d:{channel_id:42}}`, plus every opcode in OP with `d` absent — each row driving a REAL `ws` socket (not FakeWs, whose `fire()` re-throws into the test rather than into the emitter) with a `process.on('uncaughtException')` spy asserted empty, and asserting the plugin's REST half still answers afterwards. Give FakeWs a `serverSendRaw` that mimics emitter delivery so the cheap fake-timer suites can carry the same table. Existing tests too narrow: wire-contract.test.ts and gateway-reconnect.test.ts only ever send well-formed frames.

summary: `fetchSince`'s multi-page forward walk (limit > 100 with more than a page of messages after `since`) has no assertion on the messages it returns anywhere in the suite. A mutation that advances `after` to the page's OLDEST id instead of its newest keeps all 374 tests green while returning duplicated, non-monotonic messages.
failure: Mutated line 468 from `after = ascending.at(-1)!.id;` to `after = ascending[0]!.id;` and ran the full package suite: 374 passed. A repro test (250 messages posted after `since`, `fetchRecent({topic, since, limit: 1000})`) then showed the mutant returning m0,m1,…m99, m1,m2,…m100, … — duplicated backendMsgIds and a cursor that goes backwards inside one page. That is a direct violation of DESIGN §6 (dedup on backendMsgId, monotonic cursor per topic) shipping undetected. The nearest existing cells only count pages and wall-clock: blocking-budget.test.ts's 'since, limit 1000 (10 full pages)' asserts timing, and rest-contract.test.ts's 'requested limit vs the provider page cap' table exercises only the `before`-paging no-`since` branch. The conformance suite's 'paging from a cursor with limit' pages at the CORE level with a small per-call limit, so the intra-call walk never runs more than one data page.
remediation: No production fix needed — the shipped line is correct. Close the coverage hole so it stays that way.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a plugin that pages internally to satisfy one `limit` must return each message exactly once, in ascending cursor order, with `nextCursor === messages.at(-1).cursor`. Add a table over (messages-after-since × requested limit) that straddles the 100-per-page cap on both sides — e.g. counts {1, 99, 100, 101, 250, 350} × limits {1, 100, 101, 1000} — asserting exact content equality, `new Set(backendMsgId).size === messages.length`, strictly increasing `BigInt(cursor)`, and the nextCursor identity. Better still, lift it into packages/conformance so every backend that pages internally (Discord, Telegram, Matrix, Slack) is covered by construction: raise the suite's PAGING_VOLUME above the tightest provider page cap, or add a `providerPageCap` field to the context so the suite can generate a volume that forces a multi-page intra-call walk.

summary: `encodeURIComponent` on the channel-id path segment is the only thing stopping a model-supplied topic from escaping into a different Discord REST route, and no test pins it. Deleting it keeps all 374 tests green.
failure: Mutated `/channels/${encodeURIComponent(this.channelId(topic))}/messages` to interpolate the raw id: 374 passed. A repro test then showed `fetchRecent({topic: '700111/../../users/@me?x=', since: '1'})` issuing a request the fake served at `/users/@me` — i.e. the topic string steered the call to another route. This is reachable: `channelId()` returns the topic verbatim for unmapped topics (the documented zero-config path), core's Allowlist imposes no character restriction on topic strings, and a `post_topics` pattern such as `ctx-.*` admits an arbitrary caller-chosen suffix. The prototype-pollution table in rest-contract.test.ts (`constructor`, `toString`, `__proto__`) is the closest existing coverage and every one of its ids is URL-safe, so it cannot see this.
remediation: Keep the escaping; add coverage. Optionally also fail fast in `channelId()` on a topic that is not a plausible snowflake, so a mis-typed topic is an error rather than a 404 the operator has to interpret.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a caller-supplied topic must never alter the SHAPE of the provider request. Add a table of url-hostile topic strings — `a/b`, `x/../../users/@me`, `x?limit=1`, `x#frag`, `x%2F`, `x&after=0`, a topic with a space, and one with a non-ASCII character — crossed with every entry point that builds a path (`post`, `fetchRecent` with and without `since`, blocking `fetchRecent`, `subscribe`) and asserting on the fake's recorded request paths: exactly one request, its path matching `^/api/v10/channels/[^/?#]+(/messages)?`, and zero requests to `/users/@me` or `/gateway/bot`. Drive it off the same list for `channel_map` values as well as literal topics.

summary: `warn()`'s newline scrub is dead as far as the suite can tell: the test that asserts a one-line diagnostic passes with the scrub deleted, because net-util's `sanitizeBody` already stripped the newline upstream. The test named for the guard is measuring a different layer.
failure: Mutated line 660 from `${line.replace(/\s*\n\s*/g, ' ')}` to `${line}`: 374 passed, including rest-contract.test.ts's 'the gateway handshake diagnostic neutralizes …' cells whose stated point is `expect(lines).toHaveLength(1)` — 'a raw newline surviving out of the provider body would split it, which is how quoted text forges a second diagnostic in the operator's log'. That assertion is satisfied entirely by `sanitizeBody`, so if net-util's sanitizer changes (it has changed at least once — see the base commit's net-util fix), the guarantee silently moves to `warn()`, which is itself unverified. The scrub also handles only `\n`: a lone `\r` or a U+2028 in a diagnostic passes through unchanged.
remediation: Either drop the scrub in `warn()` and its comment (the sanitizer owns the property, and CLAUDE.md's comment rule says a comment must warn a future developer off a risky action, which this one no longer does), or keep it and give it a direct test with input that does NOT come through `sanitizeBody`. Prefer the second and widen the character class to all line terminators (`/[\r\n  ]+/g`).
testUpgrade: CLASS: a one-line-diagnostic guarantee must be pinned at the layer that owns it. Add a unit table calling the plugin's warn path (or an exported `oneLine` helper) directly with `\n`, `\r\n`, `\r`, ` `, ` `, and leading/trailing whitespace, asserting exactly one trailing newline in the written string. Independently, parameterize the existing hostile-body cells over a diagnostic source that bypasses `sanitizeBody` — e.g. a `fetch` rejection whose `Error.message` contains a newline, and a `channel_map` value containing one — so the two layers can fail independently.

summary: Nothing asserts that a closed socket releases its heartbeat interval before `disconnect()`. Deleting the `clearInterval` / `heartbeats.delete` from the close handler keeps all 374 tests green, even though the surviving intervals are exactly what the `heartbeats` Set's comment exists to manage.
failure: Mutated the close handler to `heartbeat = undefined;` only, dropping `clearInterval(heartbeat); this.heartbeats.delete(heartbeat);`: 374 passed. Under that mutant a flapping gateway leaks one live `setInterval` per reconnect — 720 of them per day at the ladder's ceiling — each keeping the Node event loop alive so the process cannot exit on stdin EOF (cli.ts relies on `shutdown()` finishing), and `this.heartbeats` grows without bound until the next `connect()`/`disconnect()`. long-poll.test.ts's `expect(vi.getTimerCount()).toBe(0)` only runs AFTER `disconnect()`, which clears the whole Set and so hides a per-close leak; gateway-reconnect.test.ts counts dials and sockets, never timers.
remediation: No production fix needed. Assert timer quiescence at the reconnect boundary, not only at teardown.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every per-socket resource must be released by the event that ends that socket, not only by teardown. Add a table over the ways one socket ends — server close 1006, terminal close 4014, op 7 RECONNECT, op 9 INVALID_SESSION, handshake-watchdog `terminate()`, and a zombie (missed HEARTBEAT_ACK) — each driving N=3 successive close/reopen cycles and asserting, WITHOUT calling disconnect(), that `vi.getTimerCount()` (minus the known pending reconnect timer) and the plugin's private `heartbeats.size` stay bounded by 1 rather than growing with the cycle count.

summary: The cursor a `since`-less `fetchRecent` returns for an EMPTY topic is a value the plugin invents (`'0'`) and nothing in the package or conformance suite pins it. A mutation to a far-future snowflake keeps all 374 tests green while permanently silencing the topic.
failure: Mutated `nextCursor: messages.at(-1)?.cursor ?? asCursor('0')` to `asCursor('999999999999999999')`: 374 passed. Under that mutant, core's catch-up on a topic whose channel is empty at first read persists a cursor ahead of every snowflake Discord will mint for years, and every subsequent `?after=` query returns nothing — the topic goes permanently silent with no error, which is the exact failure mode DESIGN §6 makes the cursor contract to prevent. The conformance suite has 'a since-less fetch returns the NEWEST messages' and 'since at the tail returns empty and a stable cursor', but neither covers a since-less fetch on a topic with no messages at all, so the fabricated value is unconstrained on every backend that has to mint one.
remediation: No production fix needed — `'0'` is the safe (replay-everything) choice. Pin it, and pin the property rather than the literal.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a plugin that must MINT a cursor because the backend gave it none must mint one that is replayable, never one ahead of the topic. Add a conformance case: on a fresh empty topic, take `c0 = fetchRecent({topic}).nextCursor`, then post three messages, then assert `fetchRecent({topic, since: c0}).messages` returns all three in order — so any minted value that skips past future messages fails on every backend. Cross it with `limit` values {1, 100, 1000} and with a second call before any post, asserting the minted cursor is stable across calls.

summary: Nothing counts the REST requests a blocking `fetchRecent` issues. Dropping the deadline half of the post-wake guard keeps all 374 tests green, even though it makes every long-poll that times out fire a second, pointless page query against a rate-limited bot token.
failure: Mutated `if (this.stopped || Date.now() >= deadline) return first;` to `if (this.stopped) return first;`: 374 passed. Under that mutant a long-poll whose waiter fired by TIMEOUT (not by MESSAGE_CREATE) falls through to a second `fetchWithin`, which `pageWithin` runs anyway because page 0 gets the MIN_QUERY_BUDGET_MS floor — doubling the REST call rate of core's 250 ms poll fallback on a provider whose global rate limits routinely ask for more than the call's whole budget (this package's own README calls that out as the operator's main failure mode). blocking-budget.test.ts asserts elapsed time with a 900 ms slack that absorbs one extra localhost round trip, and long-poll.test.ts's timeout cell runs under fake timers with a stubbed `fetch`, so neither can see the extra query.
remediation: No production fix needed. Make request count a first-class assertion of the long-poll table.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a long-poll's REST cost must be a function of wakeups, not of the budget. Extend the existing long-poll tables with a request-count axis using `fake.requestCount('/messages')`: exactly 1 query when the call times out with nothing arriving; exactly 2 when a MESSAGE_CREATE wakes it; exactly 1 when the socket dies mid-wait; exactly 1 when the transport was never live. Parameterize over blockMs {1, 50, 1500} so a floor that leaks past the deadline shows up as an extra count rather than as slack-absorbed latency.

summary: The `disconnect: warning` rotation deliberately runs two Socket Mode sockets at once, but the plugin only ever tracks one (`this.ws`) and only ever closes that one. The pre-rotation socket is never closed by the plugin at all — the suite models Slack closing it (`fake.dropOldestSocket()`), so a `disconnect()` inside the ~10 s grace, or a vendor/edge that does not close its half, leaks an established websocket against the ~10-connections-per-app-token cap. `disconnect()`'s own stated contract in connection-lifecycle.test.ts is "leaves no socket open", and its table never crosses the rotation state.
failure: subscribe(topic) → push `{type:'disconnect', reason:'warning'}` → wait for the replacement (fake.liveSockets === 2) → `await plugin.disconnect()` → fake.liveSockets stays 1 indefinitely (reproduced: `AssertionError: sockets left open after disconnect: expected 1 to be +0`). The orphan also keeps acking envelopes to Slack after teardown, so those payloads are marked delivered by a bridge that has cleared its routes.
remediation: Track every socket the plugin opens in a `Set<WebSocket>` (add in `openSocket`, remove in its `close` handler) and close them all in `disconnect()`. Separately, own the end of the grace: when the replacement's `hello` lands, arm a bounded timer that closes the rotated-out socket rather than depending on the vendor to close it.
testUpgrade: Add a `socketState` axis to the existing `slack teardown racing an in-flight connect` table — `{cold, establishing, established, rotating}` — and assert `fake.liveSockets === 0` after `disconnect()` for every row (rotating = push a `warning` and wait for liveSockets === 2 first). Add one row where the fake never closes the old half, asserting the overlap window is bounded by the plugin. Class: any state in which the plugin holds more sockets than the single field its teardown reads.

summary: `post` carefully refuses to brand an `ok:true` reply that carries no usable `ts` ("Slack chat.postMessage returned no usable ts…", ratcheted by a 6-row table in hostile-input.test.ts), but the same class is unguarded at the other three call sites and at the JSON parse itself. `api()` does `await res.json()` with no guard and hands the result back unvalidated, so a 200 that is not Slack's shape surfaces as an engine-level TypeError/SyntaxError naming neither the method nor the plugin — and on `conversations.history` it repeats on every catch-up, which is the wedged-topic shape the same test file exists to prevent.
failure: Reproduced against a purpose-built 200-responder: `{ok:true}` from users.lookupByEmail → `resolveIdentity('a@b.c')` rejects with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')`; `{ok:true, messages:{a:1}}` → `fetchRecent` rejects with `TypeError: (resp.messages ?? []).filter is not a function`; a `text/html` 200 body (captive portal / proxy error page) → both `fetchRecent` and `post` reject with `SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<', "<html>capt"... is not valid JSON`; `{ok:true}` from apps.connections.open → `subscribe` rejects with `SyntaxError: Invalid URL: undefined`.
remediation: Guard the response shape where it is consumed, with the same named-error style `post` already uses: reject `conversations.history` unless `messages` is an array, `users.lookupByEmail` unless `user.id` is a non-empty string, `apps.connections.open` unless `url` is a `wss:`/`ws:` string. Wrap the `res.json()` in `api()` so a non-JSON 200 becomes `Slack <method> → non-JSON body: …` (body already bounded and sanitized by net-util).
testUpgrade: Widen `slack post: an ok:true reply is not a promise that ts is there` into a table over (method, malformed body): {chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.lookupByEmail, apps.connections.open} × {field absent, field wrong type, field null, non-JSON 200, empty body}, asserting every row rejects with a message containing the Slack method name. Class: every field the plugin reads out of an `ok:true` envelope.

summary: `channel_map` is validated fail-fast at `connect` by `requireUsableChannelMap` (rejects non-string/empty targets, naming the topic) and there is a table pinning that. Its sibling `mention_map` gets only `ownEntriesOnly` — no value validation — yet its values become `Message.senderHandle` directly (`mentionMap[id] ?? id`). A blank or non-string value therefore reintroduces exactly the malformed handle that `senderOf`'s `'unknown'` fallback exists to prevent, and does so silently at load time.
failure: `mention_map: {U0EMPTY: ""}` → every message from U0EMPTY arrives with `senderHandle: ''` (the empty peer core's identity filter and roster read) and its mention markup renders as a bare `@`. `mention_map: {U0OBJ: {a:1}}` (legal YAML, unvalidated by core since backend_config is opaque) → `typeof m.senderHandle === 'object'` crossing the seam under a branded-string type, content `hi @[object Object]`. `mention_map: {U0NUM: 42}` → `senderHandle` is a number and `mentions: ["42"]`. All three reproduced.
remediation: Validate `mention_map` at `connect` with the same shape and error style as `requireUsableChannelMap`: reject any value that is not a non-empty string, naming the offending id.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `rejects a channel_map target that is not a channel id` case over BOTH config maps: {channel_map, mention_map} × {null, 42, {}, [], ''}, asserting `connect` rejects naming the key. Class: every `Record<string,string>` in backend_config whose values reach a Message field or the wire.

summary: `runFetch` computes the no-`since` window as `events.slice(-limit)`, and `slice(-0)` is `slice(0)` — the whole array. A `limit` of 0 therefore returns a full page instead of nothing, and a negative limit returns an arbitrary subset (`slice(5)` for -5). Core's schemas happen to clamp `limit` to a positive int, so nothing in-tree reaches it, but the seam declares `limit?: number` with no floor and this is the plugin's own contract to keep. The same input is the only thing that makes `emptyCursor`'s `exhausted` parameter false: I mutated the call site to a hard-coded `true` and the whole 453-test suite stayed green, so that guard and the comment justifying it ("a walk which stopped early can never advance the cursor") describe a branch the code's own structure makes unreachable for every legal limit.
failure: `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 0})` on a 30-message channel returns 30 messages (asked for 0); `fetchRecent({topic, limit: -5})` returns 25 messages, and with `since` returns 25 while silently dropping the newest 5. Reproduced. Separately, mutating `emptyCursor(args, newestSeenTs, pageCursor === undefined)` to `emptyCursor(args, newestSeenTs, true)` leaves the suite green (453/453), proving the false arm is dead.
remediation: Normalize once at the top of `runFetch`: `const limit = Math.max(1, Math.trunc(args.limit ?? 100))` — or reject a non-positive `limit` fail-fast. Then either delete the now-provably-dead `exhausted` parameter and its comment, or keep it and add the case that makes it live.
testUpgrade: Add a `limit` boundary row set to the catch-up window table — {-1, 0, 1, 2, default} × {since, no-since} — asserting `messages.length <= max(1, limit)` and that `nextCursor` is replayable, so the class (a seam argument used in arithmetic without a floor) is covered for any future arithmetic over `limit`. The existing LIMITS table starts at 1 and so cannot see it.

summary: The "cursor was minted by another store file" guard is only a high-water comparison, so it stops firing the moment a reset store's observation sequence climbs back past the stale cursor — and then fetchRecent silently returns a short page instead of failing. The store's sequence space has no identity of its own, so a cursor from a previous store file becomes indistinguishable from one this store issued.
failure: Post a,b,c,d,e -> cursor '5'. disconnect, delete store_path (or point at a fresh one), reconnect, then 10 new messages n1..n10 arrive (seqs 1..10). fetchRecent({topic, since:'5'}) returns ['n6'..'n10'] and nextCursor '10' — n1..n5 are silently skipped forever. Reproduced: expected 10 messages, got 5. Because the Bot API has no history endpoint, nothing downstream can ever recover them. The README claims exactly the opposite: "fails loudly ... rather than answering with a permanently short page".
remediation: Give the store file an identity: write a random epoch id into the file on creation (alongside the existing '#evicted' header line) and either encode it in the cursor ('<epoch>.<seq>') or carry it beside the seq and reject any `since` whose epoch is not this store's, regardless of high-water. Keep the high-water check as a second, weaker guard.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `telegram cursor across the store lifecycle` damage table over a second axis — {check immediately, check after N new messages have refilled the sequence past the held cursor} — with N drawn from {1, cursor, cursor+5, 2*cursor}. Every cell must end in either "throws" or "returns every message observed after the cursor exactly once"; a short page is never acceptable. The current table only ever asserts the immediately-after-damage moment, so it cannot distinguish a permanent guard from a temporary one.

summary: `served` is rebuilt on every connect from `chat_map` only, while at runtime `chatIdFor` calls `store.serve()` for any topic a seam call names. So a chat protected from the chat cap in one run is unprotected at load in the next, and `applyChatCap()` evicts its records — permanent, unbackfillable history loss for a topic in the operator's `topics` allowlist that is not also in `chat_map`.
failure: connect with `observed_max_chats: 2`, no chat_map. post to numeric topics A, B, C (all become 'served', so the runtime cap is bypassed and all three are retained). disconnect, reconnect with the same config: `served` is empty, `applyChatCap()` evicts the least-recently-active chat, and `fetchRecent({topic: A})` returns [] where it returned 1 message before the restart. Reproduced.
remediation: Persist the served set with the store (a header line like the existing '#evicted' line) so a chat a seam call registered stays protected across restarts, or make `applyChatCap()` at load defer eviction until the connect's topic resolutions have run. Either way, stop letting `serve()` bypass the cap unboundedly — cap the served set too, or the promised bound is not a bound.
testUpgrade: Extend the `telegram unconfigured-chat ingest` starvation table with a `restart` axis: for each of {chat_map-named, seam-call-named (post/fetchRecent/subscribe), never-named} x {flood before, flood after} x {same process, after a cold restart}, assert the operator message is still fetchable. Also add a store-level property: after load, `byChat.size <= maxChats + |served-at-construction|` and no chat named in a previous run's seam calls has lost records.

summary: Two shipped claims about the chat cap are false. README: "The chat cap never evicts a chat this bridge serves — one a `chat_map` entry resolves to, or one a seam call has named — on load or at runtime" — the "on load" half does not hold for a seam-call-named chat across a restart. And README's `observed_max_chats` row ("Max distinct chats kept in the store") plus store.ts's class doc ("Across chats at most maxChats are retained") are false at runtime, because `admit()` returns true unconditionally for a served chat.
failure: With `observed_max_chats: 2` and no `chat_map`, posting to three numeric topics retains three chats (documented max: 2). Restarting then evicts one of them despite the README's "on load or at runtime" promise. An operator sizing disk/RAM from the documented cap, or trusting the never-evict promise for a `topics` entry, is misled in both directions.
remediation: Fix the code (see the two correctness findings) and then restate both rows to match: name the residual limit explicitly, i.e. that the cap bounds unserved chats and that served protection is (or is not) durable across restarts.
testUpgrade: Add a docs lint in the existing `docs.test.ts` style that drives the claim rather than reading it: for each README sentence asserting an absolute (`never evicts`, `at most`, `max distinct`), bind it to an executed scenario table cell — here, a parameterized {runtime, after-restart} x {chat_map-named, seam-named, unserved} matrix whose observed retention is compared against the documented cap. A prose-only assertion of an absolute must fail the lint if no cell exercises it.

summary: Every cell of the store-damage table asserts only that the very next `fetchRecent` throws; none posts new messages after the damage and re-checks. The guard is therefore counted as coverage for the claim "a lost store file invalidates every outstanding cursor" while only proving "...for as long as the new store stays shorter than the old cursor" — which is how the silent-short-page defect above shipped green.
failure: Deleting the `expect(...).rejects.toThrow(/ahead of every message/)` assertions and replacing them with a guard that only fires while `highWater() === 0` would keep the entire table green, because no cell ever refills the store past the held cursor. Conversely, the real defect (returns ['n6'..'n10'] for since='5' after a wipe+refill) is invisible to every existing cell.
remediation: After each damage case, post K new messages and assert the outcome is still one of {throws, returns every post-cursor message exactly once} — never a short page. Sweep K across the held cursor value.
testUpgrade: Turn the damage table into a two-axis product: damage x refill-depth (0, 1, cursor-1, cursor, cursor+5). The invariant to assert per cell is the one the file's own header states — "every message after that cursor is returned exactly once, or the call fails loudly" — computed from the messages actually posted after the damage, rather than a hard-coded expected list.

summary: `ingest` computes `new Date(msg.date * 1000).toISOString()` without validating `date`, while `requireSentMessage` explicitly validates the sibling fields `message_id` and `chat.id`. A message object missing (or carrying a non-numeric) `date` raises a contextless `RangeError: Invalid time value` — precisely the outcome the package's own `unwrapEnvelope` doc says it exists to prevent.
failure: An update whose message carries `message_id`, `chat.id` and `text` but no `date` (a non-conforming local Bot API server, a rewriting middlebox) makes `ingest` throw. On the inbound path the poll loop swallows it into a throttled `dropped update N: Invalid time value` line — one line a minute for a whole class of permanently lost messages, with nothing naming the missing field. Verified: `new Date(undefined*1000).toISOString()` throws RangeError.
remediation: Validate `date` where the other fields of the same object are validated, and fall back to a labelled error naming the endpoint and the field (or to the ingest wall-clock) rather than letting Date arithmetic produce the diagnostic.
testUpgrade: A parameterized 'non-conforming message object' table driven through `injectRawUpdate` and through a malformed `sendMessage` result: for each required field {message_id, chat, chat.id, date} x {absent, null, wrong type}, assert the failure names the endpoint and the field, and that the ingestion loop survives. The existing `envelope.test.ts` covers the envelope layer only, so no cell of the message layer is exercised.

summary: `fetchOnce` rethrows the RAW error whenever the caller's signal happens to be aborted, bypassing label + redactUrls + sanitizeBody. The check tests the SIGNAL's state, not whether the thrown error IS the abort, so any transport failure that races a plugin's disconnect() leaks the credential-bearing request URL into model context.
failure: fetchWithRetry('https://api.example.test/bot123:SECRET-CANARY-9f3a/getUpdates', {signal: c.signal}, {label:'L',...}) where fetch aborts c and then rejects with `TypeError: request to <url> failed: ENOTFOUND` -> rejection message is `request to https://api.example.test/bot123:SECRET-CANARY-9f3a/getUpdates failed: ENOTFOUND`. No `L → ` prefix, token unredacted. Reachable whenever a Telegram/Matrix/Zulip long-poll gets a DNS/TLS failure in the same turn its plugin tears down. Same path also lets a bare `BodyTooLargeError` escape unlabeled.
remediation: Rethrow only the abort itself: `if (init.signal?.aborted === true && (err === init.signal.reason || (err instanceof Error && err.name === 'AbortError'))) throw err;` — or, better, always rethrow `init.signal.reason` for a caller abort and let every other error fall through to the `${label} → transport: ${sanitizeBody(redactUrls(...))}` branch, so the envelope has no conditional exit at all.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the credential-leak table (SPELLINGS x VECTORS, SHAPES x LOCATIONS) over a third axis: caller-signal state at throw time — {not aborted, aborted-before-fetch, aborted-in-the-same-turn-as-the-failure}. Every cell must still assert `message.startsWith(label + ' → ')` and `not.toContain(secret)`. The existing "a caller's own abort still cancels an in-flight request" case is too narrow: it only exercises the cell where the abort IS the failure, which is the one cell the raw rethrow is correct for.

summary: The suite never grades that `backendMsgId` or `cursor` survive a reconnect. Every fetchRecent/subscribe in all 21 clauses runs on the single `ctx.plugin`; `concurrentPost` supplies independent WRITERS but never an independent READER, and no case ever disconnects and re-reads. Core dedups on `backendMsgId` and persists `nextCursor` for catch-up-on-start (DESIGN §6, CLAUDE.md definition of done), so both must be stable across processes — and nothing certifies it.
failure: A ReferencePlugin wrapper that namespaces both ids and cursors per connection (`c17#000000000042`), stripping the namespace on input, passes the whole suite 32/32 (reproduced as packages/conformance/test/probeX.test.ts). Against core this plugin re-delivers every message after a reconnect (dedup keys all changed) and a persisted cursor from a previous process carries a dead namespace. A backend that mints ids from a per-connection counter is certified conformant today.
remediation: Add a second-connection arm to the context or reuse the existing one: require the factory to expose `reconnect(): Promise<void>` (or grade through a second plugin built by `concurrentPost`'s machinery) and add a clause: post N, capture ids + nextCursor, disconnect, reconnect, then assert fetchRecent since the SAVED cursor returns exactly the messages after it with byte-identical `backendMsgId`s. Register the clause in CLAUSES and give it a BROKEN_VARIANTS control.
testUpgrade: Guard the class, not the instance: a parameterized 'the seam's identity keys are durable across a connection boundary' clause run over both {cursor, backendMsgId} x {live-push id, catch-up id}, plus a BROKEN_VARIANTS entry per key that salts it per connect(). The generator should also cover 'a cursor minted by connection A is accepted by connection B' — a plugin that throws or returns the full window on an alien cursor is the other half of the same class.

summary: The negative control enforces one variant per CLAUSE and one per Message FIELD, but not per assertion. Five cursor/limit assertions can be deleted simultaneously with the whole package — negative control included — staying green, so they count as coverage while being unfalsifiable.
failure: Deleting all five of: `expect(nextCursor).toBe(messages.at(-1)!.cursor)` (l.163), `expect(after.nextCursor).toBe(after.messages.at(-1)!.cursor)` (l.194), `expect(res.nextCursor).toBe(res.messages.at(-1)!.cursor)` (l.234), `expect(drained.nextCursor).toBe(tail)` (l.243), `expect(res.messages.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(limit)` (l.212) -> `npx vitest run packages/conformance` reports 286/286 passed, 7/7 files. The at-tail one is non-redundant: a plugin whose tail cursor DRIFTS while returning an empty page (a real shape — the absent-topic version already has a variant) is caught by nothing else, and now by nothing at all.
remediation: Add BROKEN_VARIANTS entries for the assertions, not only the clauses: (a) a nextCursor that reports the topic tail on a since-LESS page, (b) a tail cursor that drifts on a repeated at-tail read while still returning zero messages, (c) a fetchRecent that returns more rows than `limit`.
testUpgrade: Ratchet the mechanism rather than the three instances: extend negative-control.test.ts with a mutation-coverage row per (clause, assertion) pair — parse each `expect(` in a case body, and require that at least one BROKEN_VARIANTS entry's child-run failure message names that assertion's line/expression. Failing that, adopt a per-assertion `mutates` vocabulary alongside the existing Message-field one (e.g. `nextCursor-agreement`, `limit-honoured`) and assert every vocabulary term owns a variant, exactly as MESSAGE_FIELDS already does.

summary: `ROUTE_WORD = /^[A-Za-z.]+$/` exempts any path segment made only of letters and dots from redaction, at any length. It exists so Telegram's `getUpdates` and Slack's `chat.postMessage` survive in error prose, but it also exempts a long all-alphabetic or dotted (JWT-shaped) credential segment echoed alone.
failure: fetchWithRetry('https://api.example.test/api/webhooks/12345/zSXqVvNlrIWmEuBhTgKcPdJfAeRyQoUn', ...) with a 404 body echoing only the last path segment -> `L → 404: no route for zSXqVvNlrIWmEuBhTgKcPdJfAeRyQoUn`. Same for `eyJhbGciOiJIUzIINiJ.eyJzdWIiOiJhYmMifQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKFtwo`. Reproduced against the real module. The README's warning names only the SHORT-segment escape ('a path segment short enough to pass for api or v1'), so an operator has no reason to expect this one.
remediation: Make the exemption positional rather than character-class-based — a segment is routing vocabulary only if it is NOT the last segment, or only if it appears in a caller-supplied allowlist of method names — or drop the exemption and keep method names readable by redacting only the credential VALUE the caller declares. At minimum, extend the README's 'keep credentials out of' warning to name the all-alphabetic/dotted shape.
testUpgrade: Widen the SHAPES table in fetch-with-retry.test.ts from three hand-picked shapes to a generator over the credential alphabets real vendors use: {base64url, base62 alnum, all-lowercase alpha, all-mixed-case alpha, dotted three-part JWT, hex, base32} x lengths {16, 32, 68} x the existing LOCATIONS x VECTORS. Any cell that leaves the secret in the message is the class; the current table passes only because all three of its shapes happen to contain a digit or a hyphen.

summary: `beforeEach` awaits `factory()` — which has already CONNECTED the plugin — and then runs `assertConformanceContext`, which throws for a malformed fixture. `ctx` is never assigned, so `afterEach`'s `await ctx.cleanup()` throws a TypeError and the connected plugin is never disconnected. One bad capability flag orphans one live connection per case.
failure: A fixture returning `{...ctx, supportsBlockingFetch: undefined}` -> every one of the 32 cases reports TWO errors: the validator's message plus `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'cleanup')`, and 32 connected plugins are leaked. Reproduced against the reference plugin; on Matrix/Postgres/Redis that is 32 live sockets and poll loops, which is exactly how a test run hangs instead of failing cleanly.
remediation: Validate BEFORE connecting where possible, or make teardown fail-safe: keep a `raw` handle from `factory()`, and in `afterEach` do `await (ctx ?? raw)?.cleanup?.().catch(() => undefined)`. Assign `ctx` before validating, or wrap the validate in a try/finally that disconnects `raw.plugin` on rejection.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized fixture-lifecycle case to context-validation.test.ts: for each way a factory can be wrong — {invalid field, factory rejects, factory returns a non-object, cleanup rejects} — run one case of the suite against it in a child vitest and assert (a) the reported failure names the fixture problem and contains no `Cannot read properties of undefined`, and (b) the fixture's own disconnect counter incremented. That guards the class 'teardown must run whatever setup did', not just the one invalid-flag instance.

summary: Both the JSDoc and the README state that `clampBackoff` normalizes into `[DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS, MAX_BACKOFF_MS]`, i.e. a 500 ms floor. The code applies the floor only to undefined/non-finite/<=0; any positive value below 500 passes through unchanged, and the package's own test pins that pass-through.
failure: `clampBackoff(1) === 1` and `clampBackoff(50) === 50`, both outside the documented interval. A plugin building a reconnect ladder as `clampBackoff(parsedHint)` and reading the doc as 'this cannot return less than 500ms' gets a 1 ms retry loop — the exact hot-spin the JSDoc's `Number('')` rationale claims to prevent. fetch-with-retry.test.ts:922 (`[1, 1]`) pins the contradiction as intended behaviour.
remediation: Pick one and make code, JSDoc, README and test agree: either `return Math.min(Math.max(ms, DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS), MAX_BACKOFF_MS)` (matching the stated range), or restate the contract as 'ceiling at MAX_BACKOFF_MS; a positive value below DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS is returned as-is' and delete the `[a, b]` interval notation from both docs.
testUpgrade: Derive the clamp table from the documented interval instead of listing pairs: parse the `[X, Y]` names out of the README/JSDoc sentence (the package already does this for the stated-wait rule at fetch-with-retry.test.ts:1120) and property-test `clampBackoff` over a generated range — every finite input must land inside the parsed interval, every non-finite/<=0 input must equal the parsed lower bound. That way renaming or re-stating the bound cannot drift from the function again.

summary: `clampBackoff` and `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` are a documented, README-bulleted, npm-published public API with no caller anywhere in the repo, and `fetchWithRetry` is explicitly forbidden from using them. `DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS`, `DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, `MAX_ERROR_BODY`, `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` and `STOP_POLL_MS` are likewise imported by no plugin.
failure: grep across packages/bridge-{core,discord,matrix,nats,postgres,redis,slack,sqlite,telegram,xmpp,zulip}/src: clampBackoff -> 1 hit, and it is a COMMENT in bridge-zulip:1172 claiming 'the shared default and the shared ceiling stay in clampBackoff' — which is false, since the loop uses an inline DEFAULT_BACKOFF_MS and applies no ceiling at all. MAX_BACKOFF_MS -> 0 hits. So the package ships, documents and semver-commits a helper whose only trace in the codebase is a comment that misdescribes it, plus three README paragraphs and a test table explaining why the loop must never call it.
remediation: Delete `clampBackoff` and `MAX_BACKOFF_MS` (and the README bullets, constant listing, and the three defensive paragraphs about them), or land the one plugin ladder that was supposed to use them. Same question for the constants no consumer imports — export them only when a consumer needs them, since each is a semver commitment.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'every export earns its place' row to fetch-with-retry.test.ts, generated from `Object.keys(api)`: for each export, assert it is either imported by at least one package under packages/*/src (re-derived from the manifests, the same way the consumer-set rows already are) or listed in an explicit, commented `INTENTIONALLY_UNCONSUMED` set. That catches the next dead export instead of these two, and forces the decision to be recorded rather than defaulted.

summary: The since-less blocking-fetch arm offers a 19 000 ms budget and then asserts only `Date.now() - openedAt < SINCELESS_BLOCK_MS`, i.e. under the very budget it handed out. A plugin that parks for 18.9 s on every since-less `parley_fetch_recent` — the hot path for an agent with no cursor yet — is certified conformant.
failure: A plugin whose since-less blockMs handler sleeps `min(blockMs * 0.95, ...)` passes this clause on every backend. The only reason the existing BROKEN_VARIANTS control ('a fetch that parks on a since-less blockMs') fails is that it parks for exactly `min(blockMs, 20000)` = the full budget; shaving 5% off it turns the control green while the defect it models is unchanged. That also means this row is one arithmetic edit away from being a control that proves nothing.
remediation: Assert the property the comment describes — 'the plugin did not spend the budget' — as a fraction, not as the budget itself: `expect(Date.now() - openedAt).toBeLessThan(SINCELESS_BLOCK_MS / 4)` (still seconds of headroom for a loaded Matrix homeserver, but no longer satisfied by a park). Then lower SINCELESS_BLOCK_MS, which currently leaves only 1 s under vitest.config's 20 000 ms testTimeout for the rest of the case.
testUpgrade: Guard the class 'a latency bound compared against the budget that produced it': add a suite-shape row that, for every case passing `blockMs: X`, requires the accompanying elapsed-time assertion to compare against a value strictly less than X (parse the `toBeLessThan(...)` argument out of the case body — suite-shape.test.ts already parses budgets this way). Pair it with a BROKEN_VARIANTS entry that parks for a large FRACTION of the budget rather than all of it, so the control cannot be satisfied by the degenerate case alone.

summary: `OpenOptions.busyTimeoutMs` is a production API parameter no production caller ever supplies: the plugin's single call site is `openDriver(dbPath, {})` (index.ts:135), so the 5000 ms window is a hard-coded constant that only tests can vary. Meanwhile the knob that IS exposed to operators, `poll_interval_ms`, is documented as having zero correctness impact. The tuning surface is inverted: the parameter that decides whether a contended `post()` succeeds or throws is unreachable, and the one that decides nothing is configurable.
failure: The failure mode is named by the code itself (PRUNE_BATCH's comment: 'past a peer's busy_timeout their post() throws SQLITE_BUSY'). A multi-session deployment on a slow or network-backed volume where a peer holds the write lock longer than 5 s — a large first prune after enabling retention, or a checkpoint on a big WAL — surfaces `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked` out of `parley_post` to the model, and neither the config file nor an env var can widen the window; the only lever is editing plugin source. I did not reproduce an exhaustion of the 5 s window, hence PLAUSIBLE.
remediation: Either expose it as a validated `backend_config.busy_timeout_ms` alongside the other two keys (bounded, documented with its cost), or delete `OpenOptions` and inline the constant so the surface stops advertising a knob that cannot be turned. Do not leave a production parameter whose only non-default caller is a test.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a production-signature parameter with no production caller'. Add a case to test/publish-hygiene.test.ts (or a small architecture test) that, for each exported function taking an options object, asserts every declared option key appears with a non-default value at least once in `src/` outside `*.test.ts` — flagging test-only parameters as they are introduced. If the key is instead promoted to config, fold it into the config-validation boundary table described above so its accept/reject edges are graded like `poll_interval_ms` and `retention_days`.

summary: `exclusiveMam`'s forward-paging loop has no iteration cap: it exits only on `complete`, an empty page, or `limit` bodied items, so a server that answers a non-empty page whose tail id equals the `<after>` it was given spins forever inside a seam call with no timeout above it.

Feed `exclusiveMam` a MAM peer that answers every `<after>X</after>` with a non-empty page of body-less stanzas whose last `archId` is `X` and `<fin complete='false'/>`: `items.length` never grows (filtered by `hasBody`), `page.items.length !== 0`, `page.complete === false`, and `cursor = page.items.at(-1).archId === X`, so the `while (items.length < limit)` loop re-issues the identical query indefinitely. `fetchRecent` never settles; core's `fetchRecentBlocking` has a deadline for its own naps but awaits the plugin call unbounded, so the MCP `fetch_recent` hangs. summary: The README's 'Presence needs a real channel' note promises that leaving `presence.topic: parley-presence` yields an empty `parley_list_users` roster 'because the topic is genuinely absent'. That holds only if Discord answers `10003 Unknown Channel` for a non-snowflake channel id — which the in-process fake invents, because it accepts any string as a channel id.
failure: `test/fake-discord.ts` keys channels by an arbitrary string and answers `404 {"message":"Unknown Channel","code":10003}` for anything not in the map, so rest-contract.test.ts's 'the default presence topic (a non-snowflake name) is absent, not a raw HTTP failure' passes by construction. Real Discord routes `/channels/{channel.id}` through a snowflake converter; a non-numeric segment is expected to answer `404 {"message":"404: Not Found","code":0}`, which `getMessages` (line 517) deliberately classifies as a REAL failure, not `NoSuchTopicError`. If so, an operator on defaults gets an HTTP error out of `parley_list_users` and the presence heartbeat instead of the documented empty roster — and the sibling test one line below ('a 404 that is NOT Unknown Channel stays a real failure') pins exactly the branch that would fire. I could not settle it empirically: an unauthenticated probe of `GET /api/v10/channels/{abc,123,parley-presence}` returns 401 for all of them, so auth precedes routing and a bot token would be required to distinguish.
remediation: Settle it against a real bot token. If Discord answers code 0, either state in the README that the default presence topic surfaces as an HTTP failure rather than an absent topic, or make `channelId()` reject a topic that is not a valid snowflake up front with an actionable message (which also makes the mis-typed-id case fail fast instead of 404-shaped). Either way, teach the fake to reject a non-snowflake channel id the way the router does, so the test stops grading invented semantics.

Give `startFakeDiscord` a documented id-shape rule (numeric-only, matching the provider's converter) and answer `404 code 0` for anything else, then parameterize the absent-topic table over id SHAPE as well as existence: {existing snowflake, unknown snowflake, non-numeric name, empty string, oversized numeric} × {fetchRecent, fetchRecent(since), blocking fetchRecent, subscribe}, asserting NoSuchTopicError only for the unknown-snowflake rows and a named real failure for the rest. Add a README assertion that the presence paragraph's promised outcome matches whichever branch the table pins.

summary: `onEnvelope`'s comment states the ordering guarantee's justification as "Events arrive in order on the single socket, so per-channel handler invocation stays in ascending `ts` order" — but `routeEnvelope`'s `reason === 'warning'` branch deliberately establishes a second socket and keeps both serving through the grace, and `routeEnvelope` dispatches from whichever socket a payload arrives on with no ordering check. Slack routes each payload to exactly one of an app's open connections (the fixture encodes this in `deliverToOneSocket`, and multi-session-push.test.ts grades it) and guarantees nothing about ordering across connections. The seam declares ascending-cursor handler invocation a PLUGIN guarantee (bridge-core/src/seam.ts), and core's push-loop does not reorder.
failure: During the ~10 s rotation grace, Slack routes ts=…000101 to the pre-rotation socket and ts=…000102 to the replacement. Any delivery skew between the two TCP connections (a retransmit on the older one is the ordinary case) invokes the handler with …000102 before …000101 — messages reach agent context out of order on a path whose contract says they cannot. I traced this structurally rather than reproducing it: the in-process fake delivers both sockets over loopback with no per-socket latency control, so the interleaving cannot be forced with the fixture as it stands.
remediation: Restore a single-serving-socket invariant: once the replacement's `hello` lands, stop dispatching from the rotated-out socket (keep acking it until it closes), so only one connection ever feeds handlers. Alternatively gate dispatch on a per-channel high-water `ts` whenever more than one socket is live. Either way, correct the comment so it no longer names a single socket as the reason ordering holds.
testUpgrade: Give the fake per-socket delivery control (`deliverTo(index, envelope)` plus a per-socket delay), then parameterize a table over interleavings — {old-first, new-first, old-delayed, new-delayed} × {2, 5 events} — that pushes ascending `ts` values across two live sockets during a rotation and asserts the handler saw them in ascending cursor order. Class: any period in which the plugin holds more than one event source for one topic.
